text: In management commands that process, omit, or auto-import batches of items, use progressive disclosure for reporting: at default verbosity (or -v 1) emit a single trailing aggregate summary line with counts instead of per-item, per-level, or inline per-type messages (e.g., "Imported N objects" with success/failure counts, or "N objects not displayed"); if omitted/processed items span multiple models/types and a total-only count would be ambiguous, include the per-model/per-type breakdown within that same summary line. At -v 2, emit itemized per-item details, and add a "use -v 2 for details" hint when failures exist.
reason: A single aggregate summary reduces output noise while progressive disclosure keeps normal output concise and makes details/failures discoverable on demand.
category: output formatting / management command feedback (CLI verbosity)
scope: output formatting / CLI verbosity handling in Django management commands that process, omit, or auto-import objects
common_pattern: Designing verbose CLI output for Django management commands that auto-import objects: use progressive disclosure by verbosity level, format import details in Python-import style grouped by module, and always surface failures prominently.

text: When deconstructing or serializing a class whose public import path differs from its `__module__`, emit the public import path for built-in/re-exported API classes; remap only known internal modules and leave custom/unknown subclasses using their real module path, applying the same normalization consistently to sibling public classes.
reason: Prevents migrations and serialization from exposing internal module paths, keeps deconstruction behavior consistent across a public API surface, and avoids forcing users to customize serializers for custom subclasses.
common_pattern: Deconstruction/serialization should emit public import paths instead of internal `__module__` paths for built-in or re-exported API classes, remapping only known internal modules, leaving custom subclasses unchanged, and applying the normalization consistently to sibling classes in the same public API surface.

text: Do not expose JavaScript classes or constructors by assigning them to `window`; export them through the module system (or an existing registration API) instead. When classes are tightly coupled, consolidate them into the primary widget/module class rather than exporting separate globals.
reason: Global namespace pollution and implicit load-order dependencies are avoided; consumers import values explicitly, improving encapsulation and testability.
common_pattern: Avoid attaching JavaScript classes/constructors to the global `window` object; instead export them via the module system (or merge tightly coupled classes so no export is needed).

text: Declare a module's public API with the dunder `__all__` (never a plain name like `all`), and keep it aligned with the intended public surface: include every documented public class/function that is meant to be importable from the package namespace; exclude internal helpers, implementation-only classes (even if used as return-type annotations), imports made solely for side effects (e.g. signal registration), and redundant representations (export only one of a class and its singleton instances, typically the instances). Remove symbols from the public API (the import and its `__all__` entry) when they are undocumented and have no verified usages, since an `__all__` entry falsely signals a supported interface — e.g. remove `LocaleRegexProvider` from `django/urls/__init__.py`. Imports in an `__init__.py` re-export module should correspond to what is listed in `__all__`.
reason: Merges the positive and negative halves of the `__all__` public-API principle with the specific cleanup condition for undocumented, unused symbols; this keeps the required dunder convention, prevents accidental API contracts on internals, fixes Sphinx cross-reference warnings, and ensures public exports match the intended supported surface.
common_pattern: All generalizations concern the module `__all__` export list as the declaration of a module's public API surface: what belongs in it (documented/public classes and functions), what does not (internal helpers, implementation classes, side-effect imports, redundant class+instance pairs), and correct usage of the `__all__` dunder to control star imports and Sphinx documentation.

text: Load shared JavaScript assets (e.g. `admin:jsi18n`) exactly once in a common template block such as `extrahead`; do not duplicate the same script include across other blocks like `extrastyle`.
reason: Duplicate script includes cause redundant loading/execution and make template maintenance error-prone.
common_pattern: Rules about how to include JavaScript assets in shared/admin templates: avoid redundant includes and load dependency-free scripts non-blockingly. The two generalizations share the 'template script inclusion hygiene' domain but address distinct concerns (deduplication vs. async loading), so they form a loose topic cluster rather than converging on a single principle.

text: For script includes in admin templates whose JavaScript has no external dependencies or required load order, load the script with the HTML `async` attribute rather than a blocking synchronous `<script>` tag.
reason: The browser can download and execute the script without blocking HTML parsing, improving page load performance when dependency and execution-order constraints allow it.
common_pattern: Rules about how to include JavaScript assets in shared/admin templates: avoid redundant includes and load dependency-free scripts non-blockingly. The two generalizations share the 'template script inclusion hygiene' domain but address distinct concerns (deduplication vs. async loading), so they form a loose topic cluster rather than converging on a single principle.

text: When Selenium is optional, move imports such as `ActionChains` and `Keys` into the individual test methods that use them rather than keeping them at module level.
reason: This is a distinct import-scoping subpattern within Selenium tests, though it is supported by only one PR in this cluster.
common_pattern: Most generalizations converge on idiomatic Selenium test interactions: prefer simple, direct WebElement commands, avoid unnecessary ActionChains indirection, and separate element lookup from clicking when the element must be reused. One outlier concerns scoping optional Selenium imports to individual test methods.

text: When a migration serializer emits a qualified reference, it must return the matching import specifier in the imports mapping (e.g., `{'from django.db import models'}`) instead of an empty set/dict, because the string is written verbatim into migration files.
reason: Missing imports in the serializer output cause `NameError` when the generated migration is executed.
common_pattern: Django migration serializer conventions and architecture: correct fully qualified references/imports, serializer registration API and ordering, naming/class conventions, dependency boundaries, circular-import handling, wrapper serialization, and documentation.

text: When reconstructing import paths from runtime objects, only process functions and classes that expose __module__, and skip any object whose __qualname__ contains dots; dotted qualnames indicate nested classes or methods that have no valid top-level import statement.
reason: Only functions and classes carry __module__, and nested classes/methods cannot be represented as valid top-level imports. Filtering them avoids incorrect or failing import reconstruction.
common_pattern: Safe reconstruction of import statements from runtime objects requires filtering to objects that can actually be imported at top level: functions/classes with an exposed __module__ and a non-dotted __qualname__.

text: For a lightweight attribute container, prefer `types.SimpleNamespace` (with a minimal local fallback on older supported Python versions) rather than importing `argparse.Namespace` solely to hold attributes.
reason: `argparse` is semantically unrelated to general namespace storage, so importing it for that purpose misleadingly couples the utility to an unrelated module.
common_pattern: Python attribute/namespace manipulation idioms, but the cluster mixes several distinct sub-patterns: direct attribute assignment, dunder-attribute access safety/correctness, hot-path dunder performance, and lightweight namespace container choice.

text: When a relative import is used, count the dots to match the actual package depth between the importing module and the target module (e.g. a module in `polls/management/commands/` reaches `polls.models` with `...models`, not `.models`).
reason: Incorrect dot counts silently resolve to the wrong (or a nonexistent) package, because a single dot refers only to the sibling package of the current module, not the project root package.
common_pattern: Django import style: prefer absolute imports (`from django.x import ...`) over relative imports, permitting relative imports only for genuine sibling modules within the same package, and requiring correct dot-counting when relative imports are used. The docs example (Gen 5) is an application of the same principle — an absolute import is kept because the shown module is project-level, not an app sibling.

text: Treat dynamic imports as a controlled mechanism: do not use `import_string` or similar dynamic imports on values read from database or task-result storage, and when the same dynamic import pattern is repeated across call sites, extract a helper that returns the import target or imported object instead of hard-coding the string each time.
reason: Dynamic imports from stored data increase attack surface if storage is compromised or maliciously modified; repeated hard-coded dynamic import strings create duplication and inconsistency.
common_pattern: Dynamic import (`import_string`) usage: avoid it for untrusted stored data and centralize repeated legitimate dynamic import patterns.

text: Auto-discover convention-based per-app modules (e.g. `tasks.py`/`tasks` packages) using Django's existing module-loading utilities (`django.utils.module_loading.autodiscover_modules`) rather than a custom `import_module` loop, and default the discovered module name to the conventional name while allowing override via a setting or an `autodiscover_*(related_name=...)` parameter to avoid conflicts with established third-party conventions (e.g. Celery).
reason: Mirrors Django's existing `models`/`admin` autodiscovery so conventions are consistent and side-effect registrations are found automatically, avoids brittle Python-implementation-specific exception-message parsing, and the configurable name/escape hatch protects projects already using the same filename for unrelated purposes.
common_pattern: Django module discovery and import-time initialization conventions: how convention-based per-app modules are auto-imported across INSTALLED_APPS (using Django's existing module-loading utilities rather than custom logic) and where side-effecting imports belong (AppConfig.ready vs. always-importable plain modules).

text: Place shared ORM default-label and choice lookup logic in a dedicated utility module (e.g., `django/db/models/utils.py`) and import it from call sites such as `django.contrib.admin`, `django.db.models`, and `django.forms` rather than reading `django.conf.settings` directly.
reason: This centralizes transitional logic, avoids circular imports and duplicated settings lookups, and ensures consistent override behavior across the admin, model fields, reverse relations, and forms.
common_pattern: Centralize shared ORM label/choice lookups in a utility module and import from framework call sites instead of accessing settings directly.

text: Do not instantiate Django model `Field` subclasses or set class-level field attributes (e.g. `_output_field = fields.XField()`) at module import time. Since field initialization depends on Django settings, do this at runtime inside functions/methods (e.g. pass `output_field` to `__init__`), and if collection/import fails with `ImproperlyConfigured`, fix the entry point by calling `django.setup()` before other Django imports rather than adding lazy-resolution indirection.
reason: Module-level field construction triggers settings access (e.g. `DEFAULT_INDEX_TABLESPACE`) and raises `ImproperlyConfigured` before settings/app registry are configured; the correct fix is runtime construction and a properly ordered `django.setup()` call, not lazy `get_output_field()`-style workarounds.
common_pattern: Both sub-groups concern the construction/lifecycle of Django field objects: WHERE a field or its derived state is constructed (module import time vs. runtime, and per-call vs. cached). The cluster splits cleanly into two related-but-distinct concerns: (a) import-time/settings-dependent field construction, and (b) precomputing invariant derived values instead of recomputing them per call.

text: When resolving a class or module from introspection (e.g., scanning sys.modules or checking sys.argv[0]), compare the actual object or path identity instead of matching only names or path fragments: verify the class object itself, compare against the module's actual file path (e.g., module.__file__), and use normalized/absolute path comparison such as os.path.samefile or Path.resolve rather than str.endswith.
reason: Name-only matching can confuse unrelated classes with the same name, and suffix matching can false-positive on unrelated paths, be sensitive to OS separators, and fail for relative paths or symlinks. Identity/path comparisons are safer and more portable.
common_pattern: Use exact object/path identity comparisons when resolving modules or classes, rather than relying on loose string matching such as class names or path suffixes.

text: When changing deconstruct/import paths for a class family, apply the change consistently to all genuine members of that family and explicitly special-case classes that are not conceptually part of it; verify each affected class is actually importable from the target module.
reason: Consistency avoids arbitrary special-casing, mirrors established patterns for related class families, and prevents incomplete API exposure. Classes outside the family may have different semantics and should not be forced into the same treatment.
common_pattern: Refactoring import/deconstruct paths for a class family must be applied consistently to all genuine family members, while classes outside that conceptual family are handled as explicit special cases.

text: When using `reduce`, import it from `functools` (`from functools import reduce`) since it is not a built-in in Python 3.
reason: Python 3 moved `reduce` from builtins into the `functools` module; relying on the old built-in causes a `NameError`.
common_pattern: Guidance on when and how to use `functools.reduce` in Python: favor it for genuine sequence folds/merges, avoid it when a simpler expression exists, and always import it from `functools` (not the removed Python 2 built-in).

text: When adding or changing a conditional branch, guard, or helper line in Django code (e.g., a select_format/conditional-formatting hook, restart_with_reloader logic in django/utils/autoreload.py, or an isinstance/alias guard in django/db/models/sql/query.py), add a test that exercises the new branch so that removing the line causes a test failure. If the line can be deleted without any test failing, it is either redundant/dead protection (remove it, or restrict it to the code path/implementation that actually executes it) or it must be covered by a test that genuinely fails when the guard is removed. Verify reachability under the actual flag values before keeping such a guard.
reason: A line that can be removed without any test failure is effectively untested and may be accidental or unverified logic; this prevents dead code after refactoring and ensures conditional behavior is exercised rather than leaving untested branches.
common_pattern: After refactoring conditional formatting hooks, verify flag-dependent reachability: remove or narrow calls that become unreachable for most implementations, and add test coverage for the remaining implementation that still executes the hook.

text: When adding or changing selective cleanup/filtering logic in Collector.collect() (django/db/models/deletion.py) — e.g., removing only deferred SQL entries that reference a deleted index, or handling RESTRICT — add a regression test that (1) exercises the new branch and fails when the new lines are removed, and (2) asserts that non-matching entries are preserved (negative assertion), not just that targeted entries are removed.
reason: Ensures the new logic is necessary and correctly scoped, preventing untested branches from being removed as dead code and catching bugs that over-apply the filtering.
common_pattern: Guidelines for modifying and testing deletion/cleanup logic in Django's Collector.collect(), covering regression testing for selective filtering and documentation of intentional error suppression.

text: In date/time tests, add deterministic regression coverage for boundary and edge cases, and control time explicitly: mock or freeze the clock at the exact import path used by the module under test (e.g. `{module}.datetime.datetime.utcnow`), cover every operation that reads time, assert expected timezone arguments/awareness where applicable, and prefer framework-provided utilities such as `django.test.utils.freeze_time` over adding third-party dependencies like `freezegun`. Make tests deterministic across environments by avoiding reliance on the local machine's timezone or real current date, using timezone-independent values or explicit timezone control. Preserve existing intended boundary coverage rather than substituting unrelated dates, including when adapting for platform-specific date limits. Cover two-digit-year boundary conditions (e.g. the 50-year pivot and future current years); keep existing RFC boundary cases such as `31-Dec-69` and `31-Dec-70` in `test_parsing_rfc850`, correcting expectations per the RFC instead of deleting cases; month-end (Jan 31 → Feb 28), leap-year (Feb 29), and year boundaries for `timesince()`/`timeuntil()` with exact expected formatted output; and timezone-aware truncation/extraction edge cases, exercising both `is_dst=True` and `is_dst=False` for nonexistent/ambiguous local times (e.g. `test_trunc_timezone_with_nonexistent_or_ambiguous_result`, mirroring flag values across `TruncDay`/`TruncHour`) and including at least one `tzinfo` offset whose `timedelta` has non-zero minutes with an assertion on the sub-hour component (e.g. minute). When asserting on time/date-derived values (e.g. generated Date headers, cache Age headers), derive the expected value from the same standard formatting/time utility used to produce it (e.g. `email.utils.format_datetime(..., usegmt=True)`) rather than embedding a hardcoded formatted literal. Add comments explaining non-obvious hardcoded dates, mocked timestamps, elapsed intervals, DST/timezone/boundary behavior, and implicit time-dependent year interpretations.
reason: Boundary/pivot/DST/sub-hour and time-dependent cases easily regress; mocks must replace the actual reference and expected values must stay synchronized, so deterministic tests lock in intended semantics and avoid flaky/timezone-dependent failures.
scope: tests for HTTP/date parsing, date/time utilities, timezone-aware db_functions/datetime, and JS date/time test suites
common_pattern: Tests that depend on the current date/time must isolate or freeze the clock explicitly, patch the symbol at the path actually used by the code under test, match production timezone semantics, and remain deterministic across environments.

text: When an API, helper, function, factory, descriptor method, or validation wrapper accepts optional arguments, flags, or parameters, add regression tests that exercise behavior-changing non-default values and that fail if the argument/flag/parameter is removed or defaulted. Cover each relevant parameter variant, including aliases and sibling public functions, and every code branch it affects—e.g. normal and symmetrical ManyToMany descriptor paths, and validation-wrapper exclusion paths when forwarding or computing an `exclude` argument. Also cover explicit-vs-implicit/default-source precedence, empty/legacy forms, and ensure parsed/passed arguments are actually used and, for factory functions, propagated to the generated object. Use tests as the arbiter: keep or forward an argument only if a failing test demonstrates it is required; if removing or changing it does not fail a test, the parameter is not actually tested, and either the test or the API should be corrected. Default/omitted-argument paths must still pass. Conversely, when verifying default behavior, omit arguments whose values equal the documented default, avoid dedicated default-value tests when the default path is already covered by existing tests, and preserve baseline/simple default-construction tests when extending tests for new optional features.
reason: Optional arguments and flags are easy to drop, mis-default, or forward without real coverage. Non-default and context-specific branches need failing regression tests, while default-path coverage should avoid redundant explicit defaults and preserve baseline construction tests.
common_pattern: Tests involving optional arguments/defaults must distinguish behavior-changing call paths: explicitly pin non-default values, flags, fallbacks, and empty/legacy forms that should not silently regress; while default-path tests should rely on implicit defaults and avoid redundant explicit default arguments.

text: When adding test coverage for an ORM write operation or a model-manager/QuerySet method that rejects invalid field names, add equivalent tests for sibling entry points that share the same lookup/validation syntax or validation path, including e.g. create()/get_or_create() via defaults, update()/update_or_create(), save()/bulk_create()/bulk_update(), and force_insert/force_update. Include tests for both writable and read-only model properties to assert the standard invalid-field error, and include the specific argument combination that originally triggered the bug.
reason: Sibling ORM entry points often share lookup parsing or validation logic but differ in execution behavior, so testing only the changed entry point can miss regressions; property-setter cases document expected errors for non-settable attributes, and bug-specific argument combinations may be required to reproduce failures.
scope: Django ORM / model-manager tests for sibling write entry points and field-name validation
common_pattern: Test coverage for ORM write operations must span sibling write paths and parameters (save, bulk_create, bulk_update, update, update_or_create, force_insert, force_update), including the exact argument combination that originally failed, and regression tests must fail if a critical write is removed.

text: When testing binary expressions that involve None and typed values, include cases with None on both the left-hand side and the right-hand side for each compatible output-field type, so output_field resolution is verified symmetrically.
reason: Output-field resolution may depend on operand order; testing only one operand order leaves the reverse case uncovered and can miss bugs in commutative operations.
common_pattern: Symmetric test coverage for binary expressions involving None and typed values, verifying output-field resolution when None appears on either operand side.

text: When testing ORM field expression arithmetic (e.g., `F('field') * N`), include cases covering multiple numeric types (`int`, `float`, `Decimal`) and operand orders (`field * N`, `N * field`, `field / N`) so that type coercion, commutativity, and division behavior are exercised.
reason: A single `int * field` case misses type coercion, commutativity, and division behavior that can break annotation/expression handling.
common_pattern: Correct handling of numeric type coercion in Django ORM field expressions — using the explicit supported API (Cast) rather than arithmetic tricks, and exercising coercion behavior through tests across multiple numeric types and operand orders.

text: Prefer reusable custom test backend classes over `mock.patch`/mocking production backends. Define them in an importable module (e.g., `custombackend.py`) so they can be referenced by `EMAIL_PROVIDERS['...']['BACKEND']` dotted path, and add them alongside existing shared custom backends such as `ErroringEmailBackend` rather than defining them inline in the test case. Tests should assert observable send behavior rather than internal kwargs. When testing `fail_silently`/error-tolerance flags, force the underlying backend or dependency to raise (e.g., with a custom always-failing backend) and assert that no exception propagates; do not mock the real backend and assert on its call arguments, since that tests an implementation detail rather than the flag's semantics.
reason: Reusable, importable test backends are readable and less brittle than patching production internals or mutating `sys.modules`, exercise the dotted-path import used by `get_connection()`, and behavioral failure tests remain valid after refactors while directly validating that errors are swallowed.
scope: Django tests/mail and other test modules defining custom email backends; Django tests for mail/logging/middleware error tolerance
common_pattern: Testing conventions for Django mail backends: exercise the configured backend-resolution path (mail.get_connection()) and use real/shared test backend classes rather than instantiating backend classes directly or mocking internals.

text: When a test creates a model and then annotates, transforms, or truncates/converts its fields (e.g. `Trunc`, converting a `DateTimeField` to a `TimeField`), assert on the resulting transformed model attribute or annotation rather than the original input/local fixture values. This exercises the transformation logic and locks in documented behavior or bug fixes; asserting on the input variable is tautological and only re-tests construction of the input value.
reason: Asserting on the transformed output validates the code under test (annotation, truncation, or conversion logic) instead of merely re-testing the construction of the input value, ensuring documented behavior and fixes are covered by regression tests.
common_pattern: Regression tests for datetime truncation/conversion behavior should cover the documented or fixed edge case and validate the actual resulting annotation/model attribute, not the original input value.

text: Tests for loop-accumulated values (e.g. a variable built with `|=`/`+=` inside a `for` loop, including Django ORM aggregation/window code where `get_aggregation` accumulates `refs_window`/`refs_subquery`) must include multiple contributing items per call such that replacing the in-place operator with a plain assignment would make the test fail. Cover both qualifying and non-qualifying inputs, and populate any accumulator dict from the input data before iterating it. In Django's ORM aggregation/window tests (e.g. `tests/aggregation/tests.py`), include multiple window/subquery annotations plus an extra non-window aggregate such as `Count('*')` (e.g. in `test_referenced_window_requires_wrapping`) so `refs_window`/`refs_subquery` accumulate across more than one ref, and also cover downstream paths such as filtering a `Q` annotation that refers to a window function.
reason: Combines the general loop-carried accumulation testing principle with its Django ORM aggregation/window application and the added branch coverage for window-reference filtering.
common_pattern: All generalizations concern loop-carried state/accumulation — correct handling of an accumulator across iterations and the test coverage required to detect when accumulation semantics are wrong (e.g. plain assignment instead of `|=`, empty accumulator, stale previous-iteration value). Two distinct sub-patterns emerge: (a) tests must exercise multiple iterations so an assignment-vs-accumulation bug would fail, and (b) code inside the loop must inspect the current iteration's value rather than a stale accumulator value.

text: When testing CSS class rendering, check for existing tests that already cover the same behavior to avoid duplication, but ensure conditional class logic (e.g., permission-based classes) is tested for all branches.
reason: Redundant tests add maintenance burden, while missing tests allow regressions in conditional class rendering.
scope: Django forms test suite (and any template with conditional CSS classes)
common_pattern: Using CSS classes as the canonical state representation and testing conditional class rendering without redundancy.

text: When adding file upload tests, first check `tests/test_client_regress` for existing reusable coverage and extend or reuse those tests instead of creating duplicate test views under `tests/test_client/`.
reason: Reusing existing test coverage avoids duplication and keeps related regression tests in their established locations.
common_pattern: Best practices for writing and organizing file upload tests, covering both test reuse and error‑path fidelity.

text: When adding type-conditional behavior or parameter transformations that handle only one type or branch (e.g., only strings, or only when an optional argument is present), add tests for inputs that do not match that branch to cover the guard/alternate branch (e.g., an Expression where a Value is expected) and verify they pass through unchanged. When extracting or refactoring a sequence of validation/transformation steps into a helper, add a regression test locking in the relative ordering of those steps.
reason: Type guards and non-matching branches are easily overlooked; testing non-matching inputs verifies pass-through and alternate-branch behavior, and helper extraction can silently change validation/transformation ordering.
common_pattern: Tests verifying a transformation/normalization path must genuinely exercise the code under test: feed raw (pre-transformation) inputs rather than pre-applying the transformation, ensure input diverges from expected output to defeat no-op implementations, and cover pass-through/boundary branches. A secondary theme covers restructuring/refactoring transformation steps so they remain independently testable and lock in behavior.

text: New conditional branches in parsing/utility functions (e.g., handling delimiters, quoted values, or escape sequences) must be covered by unit tests that exercise the branch behavior, including edge cases such as quoted strings with embedded delimiters and escape sequences. In Django's HTTP parsing helpers in `django/utils/http.py`, exercise every condition (guards, early returns, new branches) and verify test effectiveness by confirming that removing a condition causes a test failure; use upstream CPython parameter-parsing tests (e.g., `Lib/test/test_cgi.py`) as a reference for quoted or escaped parameter cases.
reason: Untested parsing branches, especially quote/escape loops that skip delimiters inside quoted strings, are easy to leave uncovered and can hide subtle incorrect parsing behavior; mutation-style verification ensures each condition is necessary.
common_pattern: All three generalizations require test coverage for newly added conditional branches or guards in Django's HTTP parsing helpers, with emphasis on edge cases and verifying that the tests actually exercise the condition.

text: Escaping/encoding tests must exercise the escaping path with real data containing the characters the feature neutralizes (HTML special characters, raw markup, operator/syntax characters, control/DEL characters) and assert the exact expected representation: single-escaped output (e.g. `<`, `>`, `"`), escaped string literals with the implementation's formatting (e.g. uppercase `\u007F`, `\^@`, `\^_`, not raw control characters or `\u007f`), and literal decoded characters rather than HTML entities when testing decoding/normalization. If a test reveals double-escaping (e.g. `&lt;`), treat it as a bug: fix the implementation or the expectation rather than codifying the double-escaped result. Apply the same escape-sensitive case to every rendering path and argument form (e.g. direct variable, filter expression, `asvar`, non-`asvar`) rather than only one.
reason: Benign inputs or raw, differently formatted, or double-escaped expected values let tests pass even when escaping/encoding behavior is broken or mismatched, giving false coverage; double-escaping changes user-visible output and should not be documented as correct; each distinct path may reach the escaping code differently, so one path does not protect the others.
scope: tests for template tags (e.g. `{% blocktrans force_escape %}`), escaping/encoding filters, and sanitization helpers
common_pattern: Template-tag and escaping/sanitization tests must exercise the escaping path with escape-sensitive inputs (HTML markup, special/operator characters, real HTML) and assert the exact escaped output, covering every rendering/argument path — rather than passing benign plain-text inputs that pass regardless of whether escaping occurs.

text: For boundary-sensitive logic (truncation, slicing, limits, counts, ranges, time thresholds, indexing), test the exact boundary and both sides of it — a value exactly at the limit plus a value just inside and a value just outside (e.g., seconds=59 vs. the next unit, or LIMIT-1/LIMIT/LIMIT+1) — rather than values far from the boundary. For functions that accept a count, limit, or numeric range, also include degenerate/out-of-range inputs such as 0 and negative values, and for boundary fixes that special-case one value (e.g., empty/zero-length) add the parallel normal-case test. Ensure the boundary test actually exercises the boundary logic: the test must fail when the boundary adjustment/condition is removed, and fixtures/data must be large enough to reach the failing index (e.g., at least 3 items when the crash starts at index 2). If no test fails when the condition is removed, either remove the condition or add a test proving it is needed.
reason: Typical-case tests miss off-by-one and range-check errors; boundary tests must hit the exact boundary and adjacent values, cover degenerate inputs, and genuinely exercise the boundary logic so edge-case conditions are justified and silent regressions are prevented.
common_pattern: All generalizations concern how to write regression tests for boundary/off-by-one conditions: covering the exact boundary and both adjacent sides, and ensuring the test actually exercises (and justifies) the boundary logic.

text: Keep each test focused on a single operation, behavior, or endpoint: place operation-specific code in the method that directly corresponds to it (e.g., save code in `test_save_user`), split behavior tests that apply to multiple write paths into operation-suffixed methods (`test_{behavior}_{operation}`, e.g., `_save`, `_bulk_create`, `_bulk_update`), and add assertions for closely related behavior to an existing test class rather than creating a new test class for each operation. Do not combine distinct cases (e.g., different status codes) or unrelated endpoints in one test. Also verify that an assertion-driven test actually fails when the code under test is reverted so a default response such as 404 cannot produce a false pass.
reason: Isolates failures to a specific code path, improves test discoverability and readability, avoids test class/method proliferation and tied unrelated assertions, and prevents false passes that do not exercise the intended behavior.
common_pattern: Test organization: keep tests focused by aligning code with the corresponding operation, splitting multi-operation coverage into operation-suffixed methods, extending existing test classes for closely related behavior, and reusing/not duplicating shared test infrastructure.

text: Ensure every mock patcher has guaranteed teardown: prefer the context-manager form (`with mock.patch.object(...):`) or register cleanup (`self.addCleanup(patcher.stop)`), and avoid calling `.start()` manually when possible. If a shared test mixin stops a patcher in `tearDown` but a test may already have stopped it (e.g. `FuncTestMixin` / `tests/gis_tests/utils.py`), make teardown idempotent by catching the expected `RuntimeError` around `patcher.stop()` rather than adding sentinel/`None` guards or resetting the patcher attribute to `None`.
reason: A patcher started with `.start()` and not reliably stopped leaks the patched attribute into other tests, causing order-dependent failures; context-manager or cleanup registration guarantees teardown even when the test fails. When teardown may run twice, catching the expected `RuntimeError` keeps teardown simple and avoids fragile sentinel/`None` guard state.
scope: global, with project-specific guidance for shared test mixins / teardown utilities
common_pattern: Safe lifecycle management of mock patchers in tests — ensuring a patcher is always torn down exactly once, either by guaranteeing teardown (context manager / cleanup registration) or by making shared teardown idempotent when a test stops the patcher itself.

text: In parameterized test loops using `unittest`'s `self.subTest(...)`, always pass the varying loop variable as a keyword argument (e.g. `self.subTest(locale=locale)`) using the minimal, stable, distinctive identifier for the case — typically the input under test. Omit expected/actual values (and other data already printed by assertion failure output), and avoid fragile identifiers such as objects whose `str()`/`repr()` may be unstable or platform-dependent. Hoist loop-invariant values out of the loop body.
reason: Keyword-identified subtests are the whole point of subTest: they report which parameterized input failed. Using the input (not the expected value) avoids redundant noise since assertions already print expected/actual, stable identifiers prevent the label itself from causing failures, and hoisting invariants keeps cases readable.
common_pattern: Conventions for labeling `unittest.TestCase.subTest()` in parameterized test loops: always pass the varying loop variable as a keyword argument, use the minimal distinctive (and stable) identifier needed to identify the failing case, and do not duplicate values (expected/actual) that the assertion failure output already displays.

text: When an assertion helper returns multiple prefixes as a tuple (e.g. `django_file_prefixes()`), pass that tuple directly to `str.startswith()` rather than unpacking a single prefix, mirroring the production code path (the warnings package's `skip_file_prefixes`).
reason: Exercises the tuple form `str.startswith()` supports and that production warning filtering relies on, instead of only the single-string prefix path.
common_pattern: Tests that verify string prefixes should assert against the exact expected prefix value using a construct that yields a direct, informative comparison (exact-prefix assertion, sliced assertEqual, or tuple-form startswith), rather than weaker or indirect checks (regex invariants, unpacking a single prefix). Generalization 2 is a false friend: it concerns Django's `msg_prefix` assertion-message formatting, not prefix matching at all.

text: When a generated migration has no header, its body begins directly with `from django.db import migrations`; tests verifying header omission should assert this exact first line rather than a permissive regex (e.g. `^[^#\s]+`) that only rules out comments/whitespace, since such a regex would also pass for other invalid first lines like a `"""` docstring.
reason: An exact assertion is simpler, directly verifies the intended content, and cannot be satisfied by unintended output such as a docstring prefix.
common_pattern: Conventions for Django migration files: what header (generated-by comment) they should carry, how that header omission should be exposed/tested, and how test migration fixtures should be minimally and consistently formatted.

text: Version-dependent tests must explicitly branch on the supported dependency/runtime version and assert the version-appropriate behavior: use version conditionals (e.g., GDAL_VERSION, geos_version_tuple) in expectations; apply correct tuple comparisons (prefer an exclusive upper bound such as `< (3, 9)` over `<= (3, 8)`); keep guards for still-supported versions; cover adjacent boundary versions; avoid mocking the version to force unsupported features (use skipIf instead); and cite the upstream issue/commit when behavior changes. Keep non-version-dependent test inputs identical, update fixtures when dependency version changes affect formats, and make error-message assertions robust to version-specific wording.
reason: Prevents tests from hardcoding one dependency version's behavior, which would fail on other supported versions, and gives maintainers enough context to know when version gates can be removed.
scope: tests and CI for GDAL/GEOS/Python-version-dependent behavior
common_pattern: Managing external dependency/runtime version differences in tests and CI: explicitly cover affected versions, branch expectations on the dependency version, use correct version comparisons, document upstream causes, and preserve support for still-supported older versions.

text: In ORM/SQL tests, add coverage for paths that would otherwise be untested (e.g. `Exists.select_format` with `subquery=False`), but do not add SQL-column assertions that merely duplicate coverage already provided by an existing `exists()` boolean test; assert only behavior unique to the new path.
reason: Missing coverage leaves behavior unverified, while redundant assertions inflate the test surface without adding coverage and over-couple tests to SQL-generation details.
common_pattern: Django ORM handling of existence checks and the `Exists` expression across three axes: SQL generation (bare `EXISTS`, minimal projection, no redundant comparison), documentation (SQL examples reflecting real generated SQL), and testing (coverage of untested paths without duplicating existing assertions).

text: Gate JSONField/JSON-function tests with backend capability flags that match the required capability (`supports_json_field`, relevant `supports_json_*`), not narrower function-specific flags such as `has_json_object_function`. Keep JSONField key-transform tests in cross-backend suites such as `tests/indexes` rather than `tests/postgres_tests`, and treat failures on any supported backend, including PostgreSQL, as bugs to fix rather than skip.
reason: JSONField is supported across backends, so tests should be portable and gated only by the actual capability they require; incorrect or overly narrow skip conditions can hide backend portability bugs or incorrectly skip supported backends.
common_pattern: Comprehensive, non-redundant, backend-aware testing of JSONField ORM lookups/transforms and JSON database functions, including correct parameter serialization, value-type coverage, cross-backend portability, and capability-based test gating.

text: In tests that manually create a `ConnectionHandler`, pair `ensure_connection()` with a `try/finally` that calls `connections['default'].close()`.
reason: Manually acquired test connections must be released deterministically regardless of test outcome.
scope: tests that manually configure connection handling with `ConnectionHandler`
common_pattern: Correct lifecycle and scoping around Django's `ensure_connection` connection acquisition: validation should be limited to the new-connection path, and manual test acquisitions must be cleaned up deterministically.

text: In database tests that create tables with raw SQL, start from a clean state by executing `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` before `CREATE TABLE` instead of relying on `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`. This ensures a stale table from a prior run or interrupted test is removed rather than silently reused.
reason: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` can mask leftover state, so the test may run against an unexpected schema and produce misleading results. Dropping first guarantees a known starting state and validates that the CREATE itself works.
scope: database/integration test setup that creates tables with raw SQL
common_pattern: Test isolation: tests that mutate shared or persistent state — especially database schema, tables, triggers, connections, and migration bookkeeping — must guarantee cleanup/restoration even when setup or assertions fail, so state does not leak into later tests.

text: When changing date-formatting behavior, add comprehensive tests: extend the existing invalid-format specifier list rather than writing separate test methods, assert the correct error (e.g., NotImplementedError) for new format stubs, cover sibling specifier variants (e.g., both %a and %A), and exercise boundary cases such as single-digit components requiring zero-padding and isolating the dimension under test instead of asserting blanket behavior.
reason: Sibling date-format specifiers and stubs share underlying logic but can fail independently, and blanket assertions (e.g., 'microseconds are always omitted') are only valid if edge conditions like zero-padding and varying non-sub-second components are covered. Extending existing test lists and covering variants/edges keeps coverage consistent and prevents untested branches and regressions.
common_pattern: Testing date-formatting behavior in Django's dateformat module comprehensively — covering new specifiers/stubs, sibling variants, and boundary conditions — plus the related concern of keeping formatter type validation symmetric.

text: For every redirect branch or flow variant (middleware redirects, conditional redirects, password-reset confirm flows, etc.), add or update tests that assert the exact expected redirect URL, including any `next` parameter, instead of relying on a custom test-client helper to emulate the redirect behavior.
reason: Untested or helper-encoded redirect branches can regress or be reverted without detection, and they can hide surprising or incorrect destinations.
common_pattern: Redirect behavior changes and new redirect branches should be covered by tests that assert the exact expected redirect destination, rather than relying on missing coverage or custom test-client helpers.

text: When a change alters CSRF behavior, template output, or failure context, update the corresponding tests to verify the rendered output and context (e.g., accounting for additional csrfmiddlewaretoken inputs and covering new context variables such as bad_origin, forwarded_may_fix, and forwarded header values).
reason: Tests that assume a single CSRF input, unique HTML names, or a fixed context set will fail or miss coverage when CSRF templates and view contexts change.
common_pattern: Two related sub-patterns around CSRF code: (a) CSRF rejection reasons must be single-sourced through distinct REASON_* constants rather than literals or overloaded format strings, and (b) when CSRF behavior/templates change, associated tests must be updated to reflect the new context or token output.

text: Add regression tests for security-sensitive Django admin POST handling that simulate forged or unauthorized input (e.g. forged `select_across`, disallowed `field_name`, POSTing fields for objects/permissions the user cannot change) and assert the untrusted value is rejected or ignored and no protected data is leaked. Omit data for unauthorized objects/fields from the POST rather than sending the full fixture set, so the test mirrors a real request and surfaces validation bugs that full-data POSTs would mask.
reason: Admin permission checks can be bypassed by crafted POSTs; tests that exercise forged/partial POST data make the implicit security property verifiable and prevent future regressions where untrusted parameters are accidentally trusted.
common_pattern: For security-sensitive Django admin actions/views, permission-based field/parameter restrictions must be verified by regression tests that simulate forged or unauthorized POST data, asserting the server rejects or ignores the untrusted input instead of silently trusting it.

text: Tests for `Q` construction and traversal (e.g. `Q.flatten()`) must cover all supported argument forms: nested `Q` objects, keyword arguments that produce tuple `(lookup, value)` children, and non-`Q` positional arguments such as `Lookup` instances.
reason: Different argument forms exercise different internal branches; testing only nested `Q`/positional children leaves the keyword tuple branch uncovered and can hide traversal regressions.
common_pattern: Django `Q` object and QuerySet-combination conventions: how to construct Q objects (syntax), how to test Q child traversal across argument forms, and how to correctly document the QuerySet `&` operator's equivalence.

text: In tests exercising `OuterRef`-based ordering of a correlated subquery, an outer reference is constant per outer row, so a bare `.order_by(OuterRef(...))` is a no-op; the `order_by` must be an expression combining a local row field with the outer anchor (e.g. `Abs(F(<local_field>) - OuterRef(<outer_field>))`) to actually validate ordering behavior.
reason: Outer references do not vary within a correlated subquery, so ordering by one alone cannot change the selected rows or exercise the ordering path; the test must combine a local field with the outer anchor to be meaningful.
common_pattern: Correct construction and handling of correlated Django ORM subqueries using `Subquery`/`OuterRef` — both at the user-facing query/test level (prefer ORM constructs, scope the inner query to the outer reference) and at the SQL-compiler level (correctly detect and resolve references to the outer query).

text: Add regression tests for feature-gated query compilation paths that alter grouping behavior, such as implicit grouping by selected primary keys when features.allows_group_by_selected_pks is enabled. For tests requiring a non-empty group-by expression, prefer stable field-based expressions like Lower('field') over combined Value(...) expressions that may change.
reason: Conditional grouping behavior is easy to regress and should be explicitly covered.
common_pattern: Django ORM GROUP BY generation and SQL compilation: expression classes should control their own grouping participation, opaque/subquery expressions need special GROUP BY handling, backend-specific GROUP BY restrictions belong in backend compilers, and grouping compiler invariants plus feature-gated paths need tests.

text: Add regression tests for text splitting, wrapping, and whitespace-preservation helpers that cover consecutive internal spaces between non-space words (e.g., 'foo  bar'), in addition to leading/trailing whitespace and blank-string inputs — those simpler cases can pass while internal whitespace runs are silently collapsed or mis-split.
reason: Whitespace-only and blank-string tests give false confidence: split/regex logic can fail to split on multiple spaces, and HTML-rendering helpers can collapse internal runs. The internal-consecutive-space case is easy to miss and easy to regress.
scope: text-handling test suites (splitting, wrapping, whitespace-preservation helpers)
common_pattern: Regression tests for text-splitting/wrapping/whitespace-preservation helpers must explicitly cover consecutive internal whitespace between non-space words, since leading/trailing and blank-string cases pass while internal-run handling silently regresses.

text: In JavaScript test files under `js_tests/`, follow the conventions of existing sibling test files: include the standard file preamble (`/* global ... */` declarations and `'use strict';`) and obtain shared dependencies through the test harness — e.g., start test cases with `const $ = django.jQuery;` instead of adding external `<script>` tags or relying on a global `$`.
reason: Matching the existing test environment avoids loading duplicate library versions, prevents unnecessary CDN/network dependencies, keeps linting and strict-mode semantics predictable, and maintains consistency across test files.
common_pattern: JavaScript test files under `js_tests/` must follow the established conventions of sibling test files, including file preamble (globals, 'use strict') and how shared test dependencies like jQuery are accessed (via `django.jQuery`), rather than introducing ad-hoc setup like external script tags or globals.

text: For invalid-identifier handling, construct a single explicit literal invalid identifier (e.g., base64-encoded 'NOT_A_VALID_UUID') and test the layer's handling of the resulting exception, rather than deriving invalid inputs from valid objects or exhaustively enumerating invalid variants already covered by underlying field/model validation.
reason: Keeps invalid-input tests explicit and focused on the view/consumer behavior, and avoids duplicating validation logic or coupling tests to unrelated object state.
common_pattern: Test data/identifier realism: tests should use identifiers that accurately represent production shapes — either well-formed realistic IDs for valid-path assertions, or explicit literal invalid identifiers for invalid-path assertions — rather than arbitrary, malformed, or derived values.

text: In tests/admin_widgets/tests.py, test related-field/widget behavior at the most focused level using existing test infrastructure: directly instantiate RelatedFieldWidgetWrapper in RelatedFieldWidgetWrapperTests for wrapper permission/attribute behavior, and use the object's change form (not the add form) when checking rendered related-object links for related objects with primary keys that require URL quoting; avoid unnecessary Selenium tests.
reason: Merges both complementary testing tactics: using the correct form to exercise link generation and using direct unit-test instantiation instead of browser tests.
common_pattern: Both generalizations prescribe focused testing of Django admin related-field/widget behavior in tests/admin_widgets/tests.py by choosing the appropriate existing test target/form instead of heavier or misleading alternatives.

text: In Selenium tests, prefer direct element interactions: use `find_element(...).click()` when only an immediate simple click is needed, and pass a selector string rather than a bound method; if the element must be reused before clicking, assign it first and call `.click()` separately; reserve `ActionChains` for genuine multi-step or low-level input sequences.
reason: This merges the complementary guidance that direct clicks are clearer than ActionChains for simple clicks, while avoiding chaining when the element reference is needed. It also captures the syntax error of passing a bound method as a selector.
common_pattern: Most generalizations converge on idiomatic Selenium test interactions: prefer simple, direct WebElement commands, avoid unnecessary ActionChains indirection, and separate element lookup from clicking when the element must be reused. One outlier concerns scoping optional Selenium imports to individual test methods.

text: When you encounter a concrete input example — whether it comes from a helper function that only bundles example inputs, or from a reported failing case — add it as a test case (preferably in the existing table-driven test data) for the relevant function instead of leaving it in production code or only fixing the implementation.
reason: Tests directly validate behavior, provide regression coverage, and document expected behavior for future maintainers; keeping example cases out of production code reduces cruft.
common_pattern: Both generalizations advocate persisting concrete input examples (whether from bundling helper functions or from reported failing inputs) as test cases in the existing test suite, rather than leaving them in production code or only patching the implementation. The shared principle is: concrete input examples belong in tests, ensuring regression coverage and documenting expected behavior.

text: Consolidate logging-related tests in the existing `tests/logging_tests/` package, adding new test methods to existing test classes and using shared helpers (e.g., `make_log_record()`) instead of creating new standalone test classes or inlining record creation.
reason: Keeps logging tests centralized and consistent with project conventions, reuses existing setup/fixtures, avoids duplication, and improves discoverability and maintainability.
common_pattern: Consolidate logging-related tests under the established `tests/logging_tests/` package, reusing existing test classes and shared helpers rather than creating new standalone test classes or duplicating setup.

text: When adding or modifying a contenttypes migration operation (e.g., in `django/contrib/contenttypes/management/__init__.py`), add corresponding test coverage in `contenttypes_tests/test_operations.py` under the existing `ContentTypeOperationsTests` class, mirroring analogous existing tests (e.g., `test_content_type_rename_conflict`, `test_missing_content_type_rename_ignore`) to cover edge cases such as missing content types and conflict scenarios.
reason: Ensures new migration operations handle edge cases safely and maintain coverage for conflict and error paths, following the project's established test organization for contenttypes migration operations.
scope: module: django/contrib/contenttypes migration operations and contenttypes_tests
common_pattern: When adding contenttypes migration operations, ensure corresponding test coverage exists in the established test class, mirroring analogous edge-case tests.

text: Do not add speculative migration dependency logic for cases that are not exercised by tests or the reported issue; if the tests pass without the new lines, remove that code path.
reason: Keeps migration dependency generation minimal and avoids carrying untested complexity.
common_pattern: Making conditional logic in migration code explicit and self-explanatory — either by documenting the exact condition (in docs or comments) or by removing/avoiding conditions that aren't justified. The first three generalizations converge on documenting migration conditions; the fourth is a distinct sub-pattern about not introducing unjustified conditional code.

text: When testing a password-state change (e.g., setting an unusable password), assert on the persisted password field (such as `user.password`) in addition to convenience predicates like `has_usable_password()`.
reason: State predicates may pass even when the underlying stored value is wrong (encoding, prefix, format); asserting the raw field confirms the data actually persisted is correct.
common_pattern: Django auth 'password usability' handling — consistently verifying and documenting the behavior of `has_usable_password` / unusable-password storage across code, tests, and docs. Coherence is only medium: the cluster is a topical grouping (password usability), not a single principle, and it splits into genuinely distinct sub-patterns (test verification, code semantics, doc wording, versionchanged notes).

text: In `tests/admin_views/`, give each distinct password/sensitive-data scenario its own dedicated test coverage rather than relying on the general base test class: add cases for existing users starting with a usable password and with an unusable password (in addition to the new-user case) in `tests/admin_views/test_password_form.py`, and put sensitive-data POST exception tests in a dedicated `PostSensitiveDataTest` class in `tests/admin_views/tests.py` instead of the shared base class.
reason: Password-form JS toggling/warnings must be verified across all edit-user password states, and sensitive-data tests form a distinct concern that should not be mixed into broader base test classes; separating them keeps coverage complete and tests focused.
common_pattern: Organization of Django admin-view tests: distinct concerns (password-form edit-user scenarios, sensitive-data POST handling) should be covered by their own dedicated test cases or test classes rather than folded into existing base tests.

text: When writing tests that submit form or query data, construct payloads with faithful serialized values and the simplest container matching the request semantics: use a plain dict by default, use explicit choice strings such as "true"/"false" instead of Python booleans or ambiguous numeric strings, and use QueryDict only when the test specifically needs to emulate request.POST behavior.
reason: Implicit coercion and overly complex request containers hide the actual wire/form value, making tests less faithful and potentially unable to catch differences in expected serialized values.
common_pattern: Tests that submit form/query/multipart data should mirror the real serialized request semantics, use explicit request-shaped values and containers, and assert on parsed request data rather than only raw/encoded payloads.

text: For multipart upload tests where a form field and files share the same name, post through the test client using a MultiValueDict that maps the shared key to a list containing the scalar field value and file objects, then assert on parsed request.POST.getlist(name) and request.FILES.getlist(name); do not only inspect encoded bytes.
reason: This shape accurately simulates same-name field/file multipart payloads and verifies that both parsed form data and files retain all values, proving the actual fix rather than merely exercising the code path.
common_pattern: Tests that submit form/query/multipart data should mirror the real serialized request semantics, use explicit request-shaped values and containers, and assert on parsed request data rather than only raw/encoded payloads.

text: When committed test baselines exist (e.g., accessibility checker baselines), provide a dedicated script to regenerate them and document the regeneration workflow in the contributing docs.
reason: Ensures baselines can be updated reliably and reproducibly while making the workflow discoverable for contributors.
common_pattern: Committed test baselines should be maintainable: provide a dedicated regeneration script and document the regeneration workflow for contributors.

text: Test-generated artifacts (e.g., baselines, HTML reports) should be written to a configurable location outside the source tree (e.g., temp or user-home directory) and named from stable test context (e.g., the test name) rather than dynamic URL fragments, counters, or hardcoded host details.
reason: Makes artifacts traceable to the originating test, avoids order-dependent filenames when tests share URLs, allows users to customize output paths, and prevents auto-generated files from cluttering or being committed to the source tree.
common_pattern: Generated test artifacts/baselines should use stable, traceable, configurable naming and storage locations rather than dynamic URL/counter names or project source tree locations.

text: Add or update deconstruction tests whenever a model field's defaults, optional arguments, or __init__/deconstruct overrides change, asserting that deconstruct() output reflects the field's effective configuration (including dropped framework-injected defaults, preserved explicit options, and correct defaults/overrides); adjust test expectations instead of adding special-case deconstruct() logic just to satisfy tests.
reason: Deconstruction is migration-critical and easy to break, so tests must lock in the intended contract for defaults, optional arguments, and custom field overrides, and test expectations should follow intentional behavior rather than forcing deconstruct() to accommodate stale tests.
common_pattern: Model field deconstruction behavior must be covered by tests that lock in how deconstruct() handles defaults, overrides, and optional arguments; when behavior intentionally changes or stays the same, test expectations should be updated rather than adding special-case deconstruct() logic.

text: Every new public (or semi-public) class or method must ship with corresponding tests placed in the existing test module for the component it belongs to (e.g., `tests/{app}/tests.py` or the relevant backend/operations test suite). Tests must exercise the documented behavior of the new API, including edge cases and failure modes (e.g., raising `TypeError`/`ValueError`), and must not be skipped on the grounds that sibling methods are already untested.
reason: Untested new public API surface can silently regress and its documented contract (including error-raising branches) goes unverified. Direct, component-local tests make failures easier to localize, keep coverage aligned with existing test organization, and prevent ever-growing untested surface area.
common_pattern: All generalizations express the same principle: newly added public (or semi-public) classes/methods must ship with corresponding unit tests in the existing test suite for the relevant module, rather than being left untested.

text: In test model files, remove fields and model classes that are not needed by the tests they support.
reason: Keeping unused test model fields and classes adds unnecessary surface area and maintenance burden.
common_pattern: Both generalizations recommend removing test-model fields or model classes that are no longer needed by the tests, reducing unnecessary test fixture surface.

text: When fixing a bug in an existing utility function, make a minimal targeted change that preserves behavior for unaffected inputs, and add a regression test that reproduces the original failure.
reason: The two generalizations are complementary halves of the same bug-fixing practice: one requires a regression test for the original failure, while the other requires the fix itself to be narrowly scoped and non-regressive. Merging them captures the shared intent without losing either condition.
common_pattern: Safe bug-fixing in existing utility functions: keep the fix minimal and scoped, and add a regression test that reproduces the original failure.

text: In Django ORM relation tests (e.g. select_related, related managers, composite PK/ForeignObject models, null_fk tests), cover nullable foreign-key/relation configurations: include NULL parents/target FKs at various levels, set null=True on composite ForeignObject and participating source fields when nullable, and assert that rows with NULL relations are preserved via counts/select_related; when testing batching, include more than one non-null related object so the batching path is observable.
reason: Nullable relations exercise distinct join/optimization branches and have historically caused bugs where NULL rows are dropped or batching behavior is not actually tested.
scope: Django ORM test models and relation-query regression tests
common_pattern: Django ORM relation tests should exercise nullable foreign-key/relation configurations and related-object multiplicity, asserting correct join, row-count, and batching behavior.

text: Add tests for early-return guard clauses and fast paths in addition to the primary success path, verifying that the fast path and fall-through path produce identical results.
reason: Guard clauses handle edge cases and optimizations must be behavior-preserving; explicit coverage catches divergences.
common_pattern: Early-return/short-circuit guards for empty or trivial inputs: place them early to avoid unnecessary work, but after necessary validation so error behavior remains consistent; and test both the guard/fast path and the normal fall-through path.

text: In an in-memory test mail backend, store `copy.deepcopy(message)` in the outbox instead of the original message, and add a regression test that mutates the message after calling `send()` and asserts that the stored outbox copy remains unchanged.
reason: A shallow copy or direct reference allows later mutations to mutable message fields (such as `to`) to alter the captured outbox message, producing misleading test results. The regression test enforces deep-copy isolation and catches future regressions.
common_pattern: Deep-copy isolation for messages captured by an in-memory test mail backend, plus a regression test that enforces the isolation by mutating a sent message afterward.

text: In tests, connect signal receivers in setUp()/setUpTestData() and disconnect them in tearDown() using the exact same signal and sender that were connected; never use setUpClass()/tearDownClass() for per-test receivers that record state on the test instance, and never rely on a misspelled or unused cleanup method.
reason: A mismatched or missing disconnect leaves the receiver connected across tests, causing leaked state, double-counting, and cross-test contamination.
common_pattern: Testing Django signal dispatch: (1) receivers must be connected/disconnected symmetrically across setUp/tearDown to avoid leaking state, and (2) tests should assert the signal behavior under test (invocation, count, sender) explicitly in the test body using shared helpers rather than incidental implementation details.

text: In cross-database migration tests for GeneratedField, avoid bare column references such as F("field"); use a composite expression such as F("field") + F("field") so the generated column definition remains valid on Oracle.
reason: Oracle rejects bare column expressions in generated column definitions with ORA-54016, breaking cross-database test coverage.
common_pattern: Django migration/model test and autodetector rules around ForeignKey and GeneratedField dependencies: regression tests must exercise the actual dependency path, test models should reuse/gate/nullable FKs, and autodetection must order/defer dependent generated fields correctly.

text: When modifying django/http/multipartparser.py, add tests that cover both successful parsing paths and edge/error conditions, including cases such as exceeding max_header_size and handler.file_complete() returning a falsy non-None value.
reason: The cluster contains two file-specific testing requirements for multipartparser.py: one for new chunked parsing branches and error paths, and one for a falsy-but-not-None file completion branch. Both require tests for modified parsing behavior and its edge cases.
common_pattern: Changes to django/http/multipartparser.py parsing behavior must include targeted tests for both normal execution paths and edge/error conditions.

text: In tests for directory traversal whose order depends on filesystem iteration (e.g., os.walk/os.scandir), make the test deterministic by mocking the traversal API to supply a controlled sequence of (dirpath, dirnames, filenames) results instead of relying on OS ordering; use real files/directories for ordinary path/existence checks, assert the exact sequence of per-directory processing calls, and only skip if the required order cannot be produced.
reason: Real filesystem iteration order is not guaranteed across operating systems, so tests that depend on it are flaky or must be skipped. Mocking traversal APIs gives deterministic, cross-platform tests that still verify traversal logic, while real files/directories keep simpler path fixtures readable. Asserting the exact call sequence proves no directory was accidentally skipped.
common_pattern: Deterministic testing of filesystem directory traversal where native iteration order is OS-dependent and arbitrary.

text: Avoid duplicate test execution: merge test cases that are identical except for backend-specific skip decorators or input-event ordering, and ensure test-target/browser deduplication removes every repeated entry (including repeats of the first element) before running tests.
reason: Redundant tests and duplicated test targets add maintenance noise and waste execution time without increasing coverage.
common_pattern: Avoid redundant test execution by eliminating duplicate test cases and duplicate test targets before tests run.

text: Tests for expression output-field resolution and query-compilation behavior belong in the expressions test module (not aggregation tests) and should cover edge cases: composed expressions (e.g. `Excluded('field') + 1`), implicit construction paths (e.g. `values(...).query.output_field`), unresolved values both with and without an explicit `output_field`, and assertions that the resolved `output_field` equals the declared one.
reason: Expression resolution and compilation errors are expression-level concerns independent of aggregation; placing tests alongside the code they exercise keeps them discoverable and properly scoped. Edge cases like composed expressions, implicit `__init__` bypass, and unresolved values are easy to break and not covered by direct-construction tests.
common_pattern: Testing Django expression output-field resolution and compilation behavior: where such tests belong (expressions test module, not aggregation tests), and what edge cases they must cover (composed expressions, implicit construction, unresolved values, explicit vs inferred output_field).

text: In test teardown, clean up only database connections and pools created by the test itself: explicitly close any connection pool established by copied connections (using `connection.close_pool()` when available, detected via `hasattr` for cross-backend compatibility), and never close connections listed in an override map such as `connections_override`.
reason: Leaving pools open causes 'cannot drop a user which is already connected' errors and ResourceWarnings; closing overridden connections breaks in-memory SQLite tests and tears down caller-managed state.
common_pattern: Test database connection cleanup must respect ownership: explicitly close pools created by the test (e.g., via copied connections) using `close_pool()` with capability checks, while never closing overridden connections listed in `connections_override`.

text: When a value passed to `addCleanup()` must be evaluated at cleanup time (e.g., `sys.exc_info()`), wrap it in a callable/lambda so it is read when the cleanup runs; otherwise rely on `tearDown()`, whose exception context reflects the test failure rather than setup.
reason: `addCleanup()` arguments are evaluated immediately at registration time, so capturing `sys.exc_info()` in `setUp()` passes stale/incorrect exception information to the cleanup code.
common_pattern: Test resource/state cleanup should be registered with the test framework's cleanup hooks (`self.addCleanup()` for instance-level, `cls.addClassCleanup()` for class-level) immediately after the resource is created or the global/process state is mutated — rather than deferring cleanup to `tearDown`/`tearDownClass` or to code at the end of the test body — because registered callbacks still run when setup or the test itself fails, preventing leaked state from polluting later tests.

text: When testing decorator behavior, use realistic inputs and fixtures: apply the decorator to a normal named function definition (not a lambda) to exercise argument inspection, and use a simple dummy decorator in fixtures rather than dogfooding the decorator under test.
reason: Normal functions reflect realistic decorator usage while avoiding self-referential fixtures that slow readers down when tracing what the test checks.
common_pattern: Conventions for applying, placing, and maintaining decorators in test code — where decorator-related tests live, whether decorators belong on classes vs methods, and when decorators/mocks are redundant.

text: In test case classes, helper methods that return shared fixtures (e.g., a class-level auth user) should be declared as `@classmethod`s returning `cls.<fixture>` rather than `@staticmethod`s that accept the fixture as an argument; helpers that need instance state or other instance helpers must be instance methods (`def helper(self):`) and should not be `@staticmethod`.
reason: Keeps fixture ownership on the test case class, avoids threading the same fixture through helper signatures, and ensures helpers that depend on the test lifecycle (setup state, other instance helpers) can actually access it. Staticmethods bypass normal method resolution, hurting testability, mocking, and subclassing.
scope: test helper methods in unittest/Django-style test classes
common_pattern: Python method-decoration discipline: choose between @staticmethod, @classmethod, and instance methods based on whether the method actually uses `self`/instance state or `cls`/class state. The dominant converged principle is that a method which does not touch instance state should not be an instance method — it should be a @staticmethod (or @classmethod only if `cls` is genuinely needed). A distinct minority view prefers module-level functions to @staticmethod, and a test-specific sub-pattern uses classmethods to return shared class fixtures.

text: In tests, build dotted paths to symbols defined in the current test module (settings hooks, `override_settings` values, `DATABASE_ROUTERS`, etc.) from `__name__` (e.g. `f'{__name__}.<symbol>'`) instead of hardcoding the module's full dotted path as a string literal.
reason: Keeps references valid if the test module is renamed or moved, avoids string duplication/drift, and prevents diff noise when tests are relocated.
common_pattern: Conventions for how test modules import, reference, and identify code under test — constructing dotted paths, qualifying imports, placing tests, and managing lazy imports — so tests stay robust to file renames/moves and consistent with the surrounding suite style.

text: When a test group relies on an implicit precondition about the test module's name/location (e.g. module-prefix matching or a dependency on `__name__`), assert that precondition (`__name__` equals the expected path) in at least one representative test, with a comment explaining why.
reason: Without the assertion, renaming or moving the module can silently turn the group into passing-but-meaningless tests (especially negative tests that would pass for the wrong reason).
scope: test files that depend on module identity
common_pattern: Conventions for how test modules import, reference, and identify code under test — constructing dotted paths, qualifying imports, placing tests, and managing lazy imports — so tests stay robust to file renames/moves and consistent with the surrounding suite style.

text: In `docs/_ext/github_links.py`, add a test for wildcard import resolution that asserts `import_locations` from the resolved module are merged into the locator, so that removing the merge line (`self.import_locations |= locator.import_locations`) causes a test failure.
reason: Guards the merge logic that combines imported module locations and ensures the wildcard-import branch is covered.
common_pattern: Implement wildcard import resolution in docs/_ext/github_links.py by reusing existing helper functions and adding test coverage for the merge logic.

text: When testing malformed request metadata, reproduce the conditions that actually produce the malformation (e.g., duplicate headers that get comma-joined) instead of injecting the already-malformed combined value, and pair that malformed input with relevant boundary conditions such as an oversized body.
reason: Reproducing the causal condition ties the test to the real failure mode, and pairing it with boundary conditions (e.g., a too-large body) verifies the fallback path does not silently bypass size-limit enforcement.
