When two related signal-registration modules overlap (e.g. `signals.py` and `signal_handlers.py`), consolidate them into one module to avoid ambiguous naming and parallel responsibilities.
reason: Matches Django documentation terminology ('signal receivers', not 'signal handlers'), avoids the ambiguous handler/import-time-registration conflation, and keeps parallel modules from creating unclear responsibility boundaries.
common_pattern: Django signal conventions: using Django's 'receiver' terminology for signal callbacks/modules, and correctly documenting/structuring signal receiver registration (import-time side effects, AppConfig.ready deferral).

text: Avoid module filenames that shadow existing symbols. Name modules that define base classes/interfaces `base.py` rather than reusing a package/entity name that conflicts with a public package-level symbol. If a module basename matches a standard-library module, add `from __future__ import absolute_import` at the top (Python 2 compatibility) to prevent implicit relative import collisions.
reason: Prevents module names from shadowing public API or stdlib names, reducing confusion and import collisions.
scope: project; Python 2 compatibility for stdlib-collision guard
common_pattern: Avoid module filenames that shadow existing public/package or standard-library symbols; prefer conventional names and use absolute-import guards when a collision is unavoidable.

text: The namedtuple class returned by `QuerySet.values_list(named=True)` should use a generic name such as `Row`, not the queryset's model class name, because result rows may include annotations/expressions and are not necessarily model-bound.
reason: Deriving the name from `queryset.model` overstates the relationship between the row tuple and the model and can mislead users into treating it like a model instance.
common_pattern: Django ORM `QuerySet.values_list(named=True)` named-tuple behavior — its testing conventions, the generated namedtuple's type name, documentation, and interaction with `in_bulk(field_name=...)`.

text: Name bulk database/ORM operations after their precise semantics, and give any related documentation labels (anchors, section names) self-explanatory, descriptive names — e.g. use `bulk_update` (not `bulk_save`) for update-only operations, and prefer labels like `methods-not-called-on-bulk-operations` over colloquial ticket shorthand.
reason: `save()` may insert or update based on primary-key status, so a name like `bulk_save` for an update-only operation implies create-or-update behavior that does not exist; likewise colloquial ticket labels are not self-explanatory to readers of published docs. Precise naming prevents users from mis-modeling the operation.
common_pattern: Guidance for naming and documenting Django bulk/database operations: bulk operations should carry precise, self-explanatory names, and parallel bulk-operation documentation should be structurally consistent and concise.

text: When implementing composite fields/widgets or MultiWidgets, give every child component/subwidget a distinct name derived from the parent field/widget name plus its own identity: in composite fields, set each child's `.name` to its alias/component key from the composite definition (e.g. `field.name = name` in `CompositeField.__init__`), validate that child names are unique, and when generating child widget/subfield names in `get_context`, combine that name with the parent field name/prefix rather than relying on original model field names or custom child names alone. In MultiWidgets and related forms documentation/code, refer to child widgets as `subwidgets` (one word) and give each subwidget a distinct name, e.g. `{name}_{index}`, rather than sharing the parent name.
reason: Keeps composed/child widgets participating in normal `Field` behavior such as implicit `db_column` generation, avoids duplicate/ambiguous child names, prevents prefixed-form or top-level namespace collisions in rendered widgets, and keeps MultiWidget terminology consistent while distinguishing child widgets from the parent `widget`.
scope: composite field/widget implementations, especially django/db/models/fields/composite.py and composite widget get_context; django/forms documentation and code for MultiWidget subwidgets
common_pattern: Conventions, API design, and behavior rules for Django's MultiWidget and its subwidgets — terminology, per-subwidget attrs precedence, constructor shape, and value normalization.

text: Name browser tests after the behavior or event being verified (e.g. `..._on_visibilitychange`), not after the browser-specific trigger or user action used to produce it (e.g. `..._when_parent_minimized`).
reason: The name stays accurate when the triggering mechanism changes and communicates the actual regression or behavior under test.
common_pattern: Playwright/browser integration test robustness: how to handle browser- and platform-specific behavior, workarounds, and event-dependent regression tests without introducing brittle or misleading tests

text: Name upload-handler lifecycle callback methods in `django/core/files/uploadhandler.py` so they match the grammatical form and tense of existing sibling hooks (`file_complete`, `upload_complete`): use the same verb form as the established callbacks, and keep the method name symmetric with the related exception class (e.g. `StopUpload` -> `upload_stop`). The exact form should follow the established convention; the durable requirement is consistency with sibling callbacks and symmetry with the triggering exception.
reason: Consistent naming grammar across the lifecycle API improves predictability and discoverability.
common_pattern: This cluster combines two tightly related concerns about Django's upload-handler lifecycle API: (1) lifecycle hooks belong on the common FileUploadHandler base interface so the parser stays decoupled from concrete handlers, and (2) those hooks must be named consistently with existing sibling callbacks. Four of the five generalizations are about the same `upload_stop`/`upload_stopped` naming debate; two are about the interface/decoupling design.

text: Name DB-API cursor result variables according to row cardinality: use `row` for a single fetched row (`fetchone()`) or the per-row variable in a `fetchall()` loop, and reserve `rows` for a multi-row result; do not name the loop variable after a SQL column alias.
reason: Singular/plural naming accurately reflects the returned value’s cardinality and avoids confusion between row objects and SQL aliases.
common_pattern: Conventions for consuming DB-API cursor results: direct/unambiguous unpacking of fetched rows, unpacking only consumed columns, and naming result variables according to row cardinality rather than SQL aliases.

text: In pagination code and docs, use correct ellipsis-related terminology: spell the concept/APIs consistently with the intended term (e.g., 'ellipsized'/'elided' rather than 'ellipsed') and use the plural 'ellipses' when a page range contains more than one omitted-page marker.
reason: Correct spelling of ellipsis terminology keeps public API names and documentation consistent with the intended pagination vocabulary and avoids misleading descriptions of multi-marker ranges.
common_pattern: Django pagination ellipsis handling — both correct terminology/spelling for the ellipsis concept in the Paginator API and docs, and the rule for when an ellipsis marker should appear in a page range.

text: In test helper classes, name attributes that snapshot initial state during `setUpClass` with an `_initial_` prefix rather than a `_base_` prefix.
reason: `_initial_*` more clearly communicates that the value captures the state at the start of the test lifecycle, before setup operations modify it.
common_pattern: Managing class attributes created or mutated during test setup: snapshot pre-setup state, detect actual value changes rather than name-only diffs, and name initial-state snapshots clearly.

text: Use precise, consistent lifecycle-state terminology across code and comments: name state flags after the lifecycle state they represent (e.g. `ready`, `loading`, `started`) rather than after reset-able actions such as `_populate_running`, and follow existing lifecycle naming conventions like `(apps_|models_|)ready`. In comments, describe the actual lifecycle stage accurately (e.g. use "till then" when fields are initialized but not yet registered, rather than "yet").
reason: Consistent lifecycle naming clarifies that flags represent monotonic lifecycle state rather than reset-able/re-entrant guards, keeps new identifiers aligned with surrounding initialization code, and prevents ambiguity about what has and has not happened in the lifecycle.
scope: project-wide lifecycle/state terminology; especially django/apps/registry.py and similar one-time initialization lifecycle flags
common_pattern: Precise, consistent lifecycle-state terminology across both identifiers and explanatory comments, aligned with the actual object lifecycle stage.

text: Use explicit keyword arguments at call sites rather than bare positional values, and ensure the parameter names exactly match the callee's signature (including singular/plural spelling). Signal arguments must use the identifier applied consistently across the codebase, and do not assume a same-named parameter has the same semantics in the target API without verifying it. For example, when calling functions such as `cache.set` or `set_cached_value`, pass `timeout=60`, `instance=...`, `value=...` explicitly.
reason: Inconsistent or mismatched argument names and bare positional arguments obscure which value maps to which parameter, cause runtime TypeErrors, and allow overloaded parameter names to introduce subtle bugs. Explicit keyword arguments with exact names make intent self-documenting and call sites consistent.
common_pattern: Argument/parameter identifiers must be consistent across API boundaries: call-site keyword arguments should mirror the callee's signature, forwarded parameters should be checked for semantic meaning, and signal/argument names should match their identifier used throughout the codebase.

text: When defining abbreviated variants of calendar/locale data properties, name them by appending an `Abbrev` suffix to the base property name (e.g., `monthOfYear` -> `monthOfYearAbbrev`), not by prefixing the base name with `abbrev`.
reason: Suffixing keeps derived data properties grouped and sortable alongside their base property, improving discoverability and consistency within the same data structure.
scope: django/contrib/admin/static/admin/js/calendar.js (calendar locale data / similar JS data objects)
common_pattern: Correctly handling localized abbreviations: use dedicated translated abbreviation data instead of deriving abbreviations by truncating full translated strings, and name such data properties with a consistent `Abbrev` suffix.

text: In `BaseCommand`, class-level hooks that let subclasses suppress inherited/default CLI arguments should use a `suppressed_*` name (e.g. `suppressed_arguments` or `suppressed_base_arguments`) and default to an empty `set()`, not a `disabled_*` list.
reason: `suppressed` more precisely describes excluding inherited arguments, and set semantics fit an unordered collection of argument names.
common_pattern: Design of Django BaseCommand's suppressed-base-arguments API and helper for hiding inherited/shared CLI arguments from subcommand help.

text: In admin widgets, when deriving identifiers from a form field's `name`, normalize formset/inline prefixes and indices (e.g., `<formset-prefix>-<index>-<field>`) to the underlying model field name before composing identifiers such as `app_label.Model.field_name`.
reason: Using the raw widget `name` inside formsets produces invalid identifiers like `order.OrdersProducts.ordersproducts_set-15-product`.
scope: admin widgets and field identifier generation
common_pattern: Admin widgets that derive behavior or identifiers from form field names must account for formset/inline name prefixes and have explicit formset regression coverage.

text: Name internal helper methods that return options for `__repr__` with a private, purpose-specific name such as `_get_repr_options`, not a generic name like `get_options`.
reason: The leading underscore signals internal use, and the specific name clarifies the helper's role for subclass authors overriding it for `__repr__`.
common_pattern: Conventions for base-class helper methods that supply extra __init__ options for __repr__, covering both naming (private, purpose-specific) and documentation of the return contract so subclasses know what to override and return.

text: In test assertions that use transform lambdas (e.g. `assertQuerysetEqual(..., transform=lambda a: a.n1)`), use `a` as the lambda parameter name to stay consistent with the convention used across the test suite; do not introduce alternatives such as `x`.
reason: Consistent lambda parameter naming across the test suite reduces cognitive load and matches the established project style; deviations like `x` were explicitly flagged and reverted.
scope: tests, especially tests/db_functions/ and similar assertion-heavy test modules
common_pattern: Conventions for short inline lambdas used as transform callbacks in test assertions (naming of the parameter and inline placement on the same line as the preceding arguments).

text: Give distinct concerns their own dedicated, storage-neutral settings/constants rather than overloading existing cookie settings/names. Define `{FEATURE}_SESSION_KEY`-style settings for session storage (mirroring Django's `LANGUAGE_SESSION_KEY`), use a separate key per storage backend, and keep URL-facing names/tokens separate from session/storage keys. In Django CSRF, respect `CSRF_USE_SESSIONS`: resolve the cookie domain with `SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN` when sessions are enabled and `CSRF_COOKIE_DOMAIN` otherwise; when `CSRF_USE_SESSIONS` is enabled, `CSRF_COOKIE_DOMAIN` is irrelevant and should be rejected (e.g. via `ImproperlyConfigured`) with a message directing users to `SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN`; name token persistence storage-neutrally (prefer `_set_token`/`_set_secret` over `_set_csrf_cookie`) and use a dedicated `CSRF_SESSION_KEY` instead of reusing `CSRF_COOKIE_NAME`.
reason: Keeps unrelated configuration independently configurable and each value independently changeable; ensures CSRF referer validation is consistent with where CSRF state is actually stored, and avoids cookie-specific names/settings when the token may be session-backed.
scope: global; applies specifically to Django CSRF middleware/settings and related session-vs-cookie configuration
common_pattern: Django CSRF middleware internals should be named and structured storage-neutrally and with clear, side-effect-free responsibilities, because `CSRF_USE_SESSIONS` means the token can live in either a cookie or the session and helpers can be misused or mis-named. The cluster covers three related sub-themes: (a) storage-neutral naming, (b) side-effect-free getters/helpers, and (c) function names matching actual behavior.

text: Exclude auto-generated, vendored, and third-party files from style linting/formatting; if they are checked at all, enforce only syntactic validity rather than style rules such as isort or maximum line length. Lint only hand-authored source files/formats, including first-party maintained JavaScript (e.g., build/config files like `Gruntfile.js`) and documentation sources (e.g., `.rst`/`.txt`, docs CSS/JS). In config, use broad include globs to cover all hand-authored sources (e.g., `docs/**/*.css`, `docs/**/*.js` in `biome.json`) and targeted negated globs to exclude generated/build output (e.g., `!docs/_build/**`); in ESLint ignore configuration, exclude only generated, vendored, or third-party JavaScript (especially files refreshed by automated fetch/replace) and include first-party maintained JavaScript. Add specific exclusions only for vendored files that genuinely should not be formatted, and filter out generated files such as Django migrations and `.po` translation catalogs instead of special-casing them in the lint pipeline.
reason: Generated/vendored/third-party code is not maintained by hand, so style rules cause unnecessary churn, noise, and tooling complexity without improving readability. Broad includes avoid missing newly added first-party source files, while targeted excludes keep generated/build output and vendored files out of formatting/linting.
common_pattern: Lint-suppression hygiene: avoid silencing lint/format rules unless there is a genuine, unavoidable need; prefer fixing the root cause, and when a suppression is genuinely required, scope it narrowly (line/file-specific) and only for rules the project actually enforces.

text: Treat a database connection alias (`self.alias`) as the stable connection identity. When caching per-database backend resources (e.g., Django connection pools), key the cache by `self.alias` rather than mutable connection parameters such as password, `dbname`, or `conn_params`; mutable values can change at runtime (e.g., rotating passwords), creating new cache entries and causing unbounded cache growth and leaked pools. Do not overload the alias to implicitly control unrelated connection options (e.g., enabling pooling); aliases should reflect the real connection identity so database logs and introspection remain accurate.
reason: The alias is the stable per-connection identifier. Using mutable settings in cache keys leaks resources when credentials or connection parameters change, and using aliases as a side-channel for configuration is opaque and can produce misleading database logs.
scope: django/db/backends/* for per-alias resource caching; global for database connection alias semantics
common_pattern: How database connection aliases relate to connection identity — a stable, meaningful identifier that should be the basis for per-connection resource caching and that must not be overloaded with unrelated configuration semantics.

text: Validate configuration-driven conditions through Django system checks (one-time at startup/deployment) rather than emitting per-request warnings or raising ImproperlyConfigured on the per-request path. Apply this to middleware dependency/ordering checks as well as other stable, configuration-induced conditions (e.g., middleware forcing sync/async adaptation). For middleware checks, follow the style of existing admin middleware checks: keep check messages concise, name required middleware by fully qualified dotted path together with the exact ordering requirement ("X must appear before Y in MIDDLEWARE"), and do not redundantly spell out "the MIDDLEWARE setting". Gate expensive middleware lookups (e.g., _subclass_index) behind cheap presence checks to avoid unnecessary imports.
reason: Middleware ordering and other static configuration issues are frequent sources of missing request attributes or noisy console output; system checks centralize validation outside the request path, avoid per-request overhead, keep issues discoverable at startup, and concise, exact messages turn vague setup errors into concrete fixes.
scope: Django system checks for middleware and configuration validation (e.g., contrib/*/checks.py, startup diagnostics)
common_pattern: Django middleware configuration and presence handling: how to validate middleware dependencies (via system checks with concise, exact ordering/path messages rather than per-request errors or generic instructions), and how to reliably detect whether a middleware is enabled (subclass-aware, non-scanning).

text: When resolving aliases by name, reference the defined constant instead of hard-coding the literal alias string. For Django STORAGES, define the default mapping in `django/conf/global_settings.py` with alias keys `'default'` and `'staticfiles'` pointing explicitly to `django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage` and `django.contrib.staticfiles.storage.StaticFilesStorage`; use `'default'` for the primary backend. Keep alias-name constants such as `DEFAULT_STORAGE_ALIAS` and `STATICFILES_STORAGE_ALIAS` as internal constants in `django/conf/__init__.py` rather than user-configurable settings. When referring to these well-known aliases in Django code or tests, use the defined constants (e.g., `STATICFILES_STORAGE_ALIAS`) instead of duplicating string literals such as `'staticfiles'`. For the default email provider, use `DEFAULT_EMAIL_PROVIDER_ALIAS` instead of hard-coding the alias string.
reason: Keeps provider and storage alias resolution consistent, centralizes storage aliases, prepares STORAGES to stand alone when deprecated settings are removed, avoids naming inconsistencies, and prevents magic strings from desynchronizing call sites and tests from source constants.
scope: Django STORAGES and alias constant usage
common_pattern: Django STORAGES setting conventions: centralize default storage aliases in global_settings, keep alias names as internal constants, avoid duplicating alias string literals in code/tests, and test missing STORAGES aliases by replacing the whole settings dictionary.

text: Keep the canonical docs exclusion list in `docs/conf.py` (`exclude_patterns`) as the single source of truth, and mirror it in every other docs build tool (Makefile, make.bat). Update both `exclude_patterns` and the corresponding Makefile exclusion lists whenever a documentation directory such as `_static`, `_ext`, or `_theme` is added (e.g. use a generic `find ... -path './_*' -type d -prune` instead of hard-coding each directory). When Sphinx is configured with `.txt` (or other non-`.rst`) extensions in `source_suffix`, `exclude_patterns` must list every non-documentation directory (e.g. `_ext`, `_static`, asset directories) so files like `LICENSE.txt`, `requirements.txt`, or `readme.txt` inside them are not parsed as reST sources.
reason: Exclusion lists duplicated across conf.py, Makefile, and make.bat drift over time, causing Sphinx targets and direct invocations to disagree about which files are documentation sources. Additionally, Sphinx searches all files matching the configured source suffixes; without explicit exclusions, non-doc `.txt` assets in non-doc directories get misinterpreted as documentation sources, producing spurious warnings/errors.
common_pattern: Keeping documentation build exclusion patterns consistent and correctly specified across all tooling (docs/conf.py, Makefile, make.bat) so Sphinx does not misinterpret non-documentation files as reST sources.

text: Environment-variable boolean parsing helpers should normalize input case-insensitively (e.g. `str(val).lower()`) before comparison and accept common truthy spellings beyond `true`/`t`/`1` — including `y`, `yes`, and `on` — while guarding that the value is string-like. When strict parsing is desired, validate against both truthy and falsy token sets and raise `ValueError` for unrecognized values instead of silently coercing to `False`.
reason: Environment variables commonly use abbreviated or alternative truthy forms and mixed casing; rejecting `yes`/`y`/`TRUE` surprises users, and blindly coercing unknown values to `False` hides misconfiguration. Guarding with `str(val).lower()` avoids `AttributeError` when a non-string default (like `True` or `1`) is passed.
common_pattern: Correct handling of boolean values that originate from environment variables (which arrive as strings), where naive truthiness or narrow case-sensitive parsing produces surprising results — either rejecting valid truthy spellings or silently enabling options with values like "False".

text: For boolean configuration options (e.g. database backend `OPTIONS` or settings dicts) that may be populated from environment variables, compare with identity (`is True` / `is False`) instead of relying on truthiness; env-var-derived values arrive as strings, and strings such as `"False"` or `"0"` are truthy and would otherwise silently enable the option.
reason: Environment variables are always strings, so a truthiness check on `"False"` evaluates as enabled. Identity comparison fails safe and prevents mis-typed or env-sourced config from being treated as an enabled boolean flag.
scope: Boolean config options that may be sourced from environment variables
common_pattern: Correct handling of boolean values that originate from environment variables (which arrive as strings), where naive truthiness or narrow case-sensitive parsing produces surprising results — either rejecting valid truthy spellings or silently enabling options with values like "False".

text: In Django management commands that handle compressed input/output (e.g., `loaddata` and `dumpdata`), centralize compression handling in a class/instance `compression_formats` mapping keyed by filename suffix and mapped to `(open, mode)` tuples. Include every accepted extension alias (e.g., `xz`/`lzma`, `zip`) and the `None` key for uncompressed/default output so compressed and uncompressed paths share the same lookup and code path, and mirror the mapping between paired commands instead of defining per-command helper methods.
reason: A single registry keeps related commands symmetric, avoids missed aliases, avoids special-casing the no-compression path, and makes format handling easier to maintain and extend.
scope: Django management commands handling compressed input/output
common_pattern: Maintaining complete and consistent compression-format support in Django management commands across implementation, error handling, tests, and documentation.

text: When mapping a file extension to a compression library's open function (e.g., in a `compression_formats` table), pass explicit format/kwargs that reproduce the container format the extension conventionally denotes instead of relying on the library default (e.g., `.lzma` requires `format=lzma.FORMAT_ALONE` because `lzma.open()` defaults to the `.xz` container).
reason: File extensions imply a specific on-disk format and library defaults often differ; relying on defaults silently produces files whose actual format does not match their suffix, breaking readers that expect the extension's canonical format.
common_pattern: Rules governing how a file-extension→compression-open-function mapping table (compression_formats) must be defined: explicit format arguments matching each extension, a complete/uniform mapping including an uncompressed (None) entry, and keeping entries self-contained without one-off helper variables.

text: Command-line flags passed to external tools, scripts, or CI `run:` steps must exactly match the options the target actually accepts: use the correct spelling, only pass options supported by the minimum/pinned target version, and check that a flag is not already present before adding it (no duplicates).
reason: Misspelled or unsupported flags are silently ignored or cause the invocation to fail, and duplicate flags add noise and confusion, so the command does not exercise the intended option.
common_pattern: Correctness and safety of CLI argument handling in test-runner / CI tooling: flags must match the target tool's real options, user-supplied parameters must not be silently overridden, and CLI options must be covered by behavior-focused tests.

text: When a class must support both Python 2 and Python 3, apply metaclasses with the @six.add_metaclass(MetaClass) decorator instead of the __metaclass__ class attribute, which is silently ignored on Python 3.
reason: __metaclass__ only works on Python 2; six.add_metaclass provides a single cross-version-compatible form so the metaclass is actually applied on Python 3.
common_pattern: Metaclass handling in Python/Django test-case classes: these generalizations all concern how metaclasses should be implemented, applied, and named. Two of them (G1, G2) converge on the same principle of deferring to Python's native metaclass-conflict behavior; G3 covers cross-version metaclass application; G4 covers metaclass naming conventions. The shared thread is metaclass hygiene, but the sub-patterns are genuinely distinct.

text: For database backend connection initialization, handle multiple SQL statements by separating them with `;`: split incoming `init_command` values on `;` when executing them, and join generated connection-init clauses with `;` when they cannot be combined into a single statement. This preserves single-roundtrip behavior and matches existing backend conventions such as MySQL's `;`-splitting.
reason: Some drivers reject multiple statements in one execute call, while some databases reject incompatible clauses in a single statement. Emitting/parsing separate `;`-separated statements allows valid execution without extra roundtrips and keeps init-command semantics consistent across backends.
common_pattern: Connection-init SQL for database backends must support multiple statements by treating `;` as the statement separator, both when parsing user-supplied `init_command` and when generating backend-specific init SQL.

text: Keep the repository `.gitignore` limited to ignore patterns relevant to all contributors (project-generated build/test artifacts). Do not add developer-local paths — IDE/editor artifacts (`.idea/`, `.vscode/`, `*.iml`) or local virtual environment directories (`venv/`, `.venv/`, `env/`) — to the shared `.gitignore`; instead configure those in a user-level global gitignore or `.git/info/exclude`, or rely on the virtualenv tool's own internal `.gitignore`. When an environment ignore is legitimately required, use exact project-convention entries (e.g., `.venv/`) rather than broad prefix globs like `venv*/`.
reason: Shared ignore rules apply to every contributor; committing one developer's editor or environment preferences pollutes the file, hides accidental commits, causes unnecessary churn/merge conflicts, and can produce accidental broad ignores. Personal/local ignores belong in `.git/info/exclude` or a global excludes file so they only affect the local clone.
common_pattern: All generalizations converge on the same principle: a repository's shared ignore configuration (`.gitignore`) must contain only project-wide, contributor-independent ignore patterns — personal IDE/editor artifacts (`.idea/`, `.vscode/`, `*.iml`) and local environment directories (`venv/`, `.venv/`, `env/`) belong in user-level/global gitignore or `.git/info/exclude`, not in the committed project configuration.

text: In `AppConfig.ready()` loops over `connections.all()`, nest backend-specific setup under the matching `conn.vendor == '<vendor>'` guard, apply metadata configuration (e.g., `introspection.data_types_reverse`) outside `if conn.connection is not None` guards so all matching connections are updated, and apply per-connection setup to already-open connections rather than closing all connections.
reason: Vendor guards scope the logic to the intended backend and avoid redundant checks; metadata must be registered for every matching connection even before a physical connection exists; and closing connections is more likely to break transactional test state than configuring open ones.
common_pattern: Django database-backend connection/session setup: where to place initialization code (hooks vs new API, lifecycle hooks vs AppConfig.ready loops), how to scope it per-connection, and preferring programmatic enforcement over warnings.

text: When configuring the Oracle test user, grant only the specific privileges documented in Django's Oracle notes (for example, SELECT ON v$parameter) rather than aggregate roles such as SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE, and keep grants aligned with the documentation.
reason: Least-privilege grants reduce risk and ensure the test configuration matches Django's documented Oracle requirements.
common_pattern: Oracle backend maintenance: keep version/feature requirements aligned with the project's actual minimum supported versions and documented source of truth, avoid unnecessary compatibility checks, and apply least privilege to test-user grants. Version numbers in the cluster are historical/evolving floors rather than contradictory rules.

text: In pa11y/pa11y-ci configuration files such as `pa11y.json`, define URL-specific actions inside the matching object in the `urls` array using `{ "url": "...", "actions": [...] }` instead of a global top-level `actions` array. Use the object's `url` field for navigation and keep `actions` limited to post-navigation steps; omit a separate `navigate to` action for that same URL.
reason: JSON object keys are unordered, so a top-level `actions` array has no defined execution relationship with top-level `urls`. The documented per-URL object form makes the action-to-URL association explicit, avoids redundant navigation, and ensures actions run before the relevant URL is tested.
common_pattern: In pa11y/pa11y-ci configuration, URL-specific actions must be scoped to the corresponding URL object in the `urls` array rather than defined as a global top-level `actions` list; the URL object's `url` field handles navigation, so `actions` should contain only post-navigation steps.

text: For Django database backends, declare DISTINCT-aggregate support declaratively: put shared expression-support validation in `BaseDatabaseOperations.check_expression_support()` and expose backend limitations as a class-level `unsupported_distinct_aggregates` attribute on each backend's operations class. When adding or auditing an entry, cover the full set of aggregate functions and their backend SQL variants (including paired `*_POP`/`*_SAMP` implementations like `StdDev`/`Variance`), apply the same entry to every backend whose SQL functions share the limitation, and add tests for each aggregate/DISTINCT combination so omissions fail.
reason: Keeps backend-specific DISTINCT support DRY and configurable (including by third-party backends) without reimplementing check_expression_support, while preventing invalid SQL from being generated on backends that cannot honor `distinct=True`.
common_pattern: Django ORM DISTINCT/aggregate handling: declaring and validating backend-specific support for DISTINCT aggregates, and avoiding redundant or wrongly-derived DISTINCT usage when the underlying column/state is already unique or authoritative.

text: Configure Black in tox to run `black --check .` from the repository root so it discovers all Python files (package, tests, setup.py, scripts, docs) and honors .gitignore; place intentional formatting exclusions (e.g., invalid-syntax test fixtures) in `[tool.black] extend-exclude` in pyproject.toml rather than narrowing the command's target paths.
reason: Running over `.` with centralized `extend-exclude` keeps the formatter repository-wide while cleanly skipping known intentional exceptions, avoiding drift in files outside the main package and ad hoc command-path narrowing.
common_pattern: Pre-submission Python quality enforcement: running Black (and basic syntax/lint checks) so reviewers don't catch formatting or syntax errors, plus a consistent way to configure Black in CI/tox so it covers the whole repo. The cluster splits into two complementary halves: (a) contributor-side formatting/validation before submitting, and (b) project-side Black configuration (run over `.` from repo root, put exceptions in `pyproject.toml extend-exclude`).

text: Do not include translation catalog (`*.po` / `*.mo`) changes in code PRs unless they represent actual translation-content updates required by the project workflow. Avoid committing formatting-only, line-number-only, source-location (`#: file:line`), metadata (`PO-Revision-Date`), empty-`msgstr`, and compiled `.mo` changes; in Django, locale catalogs under `django/conf/locale/` are managed via Transifex by the release manager, so such changes should normally be reverted. If the workflow explicitly requires syncing catalogs after changing translatable source strings, update only the relevant `.po` entries and preserve still-valid existing translations; never hand-edit `.mo` files.
reason: Translation catalogs are noisy, externally managed localization artifacts. Committing incidental or generated changes causes conflicts with the translation workflow, while catalog updates needed for source-string changes should remain minimal and avoid invalidating valid translations.
common_pattern: Translation catalog files (`*.po` / `*.mo`) are treated as generated or externally managed localization artifacts. The cluster converges on avoiding unrelated, noisy, or hand-edited catalog changes, while a smaller sub-pattern notes that when source strings change and the workflow requires catalog synchronization, only relevant `.po` entries should be updated. There is tension between 'do not touch `.po`' and 'update `.po` for string changes'; this is best handled as a single contextual rule.

text: For optional backend/database behavior, prefer documenting a user-facing opt-in configuration over introducing a new framework-level setting; if the change is larger, defer it to a separate PR rather than bundling it here.
reason: Avoids proliferating settings for niche/optional behavior while keeping the current change focused; documented opt-in still makes the behavior explicit for users who need it.
common_pattern: All four generalizations concern how to present optional/opt-in behavior to users: three are about the phrasing of that documentation (concise, capability-framed, user-centric, scope-explained), and the fourth is about preferring documented user-facing opt-in configuration over adding new framework settings. The unifying theme is 'make opt-in behavior explicit and user-facing rather than mechanical or framework-proliferating.'

text: In `django/db/backends/mysql/schema.py`, when calculating `_max_index_size`, assume the connection uses utf8mb4 and return fixed character limits based on MySQL version rather than deriving limits from the connection charset/byte calculations: use 191 for MySQL versions before 5.7.7 and 767 for 5.7.7 and later.
reason: This simplifies backend logic, avoids incorrect assumptions from non-default charsets, and aligns with Django's default utf8mb4 charset.
common_pattern: Handling and documenting MySQL/InnoDB index key prefix length limits caused by charset byte limits, especially for `CharField`/`VARCHAR` `max_length` and unique indexes.

text: In `.github/workflows/*.yml`, explicitly set least-privilege `permissions` for `GITHUB_TOKEN`; grant a single access level per scope (`read`, `write`, or `none`) and use `write` when read+write access is needed because `write` implies `read`.
reason: Limits the token scope if a workflow is compromised and avoids invalid/redundant permission combinations such as `read|write`.
common_pattern: Repository conventions for securing and standardizing GitHub Actions workflows: least-privilege token permissions, immutable/action-version pinning, preferring official actions, and branch-scoped PR triggers. The cluster is coherent at the theme level but contains several distinct sub-patterns.

text: In middleware that resolves per-view configuration, resolve values from the view function/decorated callable first, use global settings or middleware defaults only as a fallback, and do not retain view_class/class-attribute compatibility branches once the codebase has migrated to function/decorator-level attributes.
reason: View-specific configuration should override global middleware defaults, and removing stale class-level fallback code prevents dead compatibility code from masking view-specific behavior or implying unsupported class-attribute resolution.
common_pattern: Per-view configuration resolution in middleware should prefer values defined on the view function/decorated callable over middleware defaults, and stale class-level/view_class compatibility fallbacks should be removed after migration to function-level attributes. Generalizations 2 and 3 are complementary cleanup details supporting the same precedence principle as Generalization 1.

text: For setuptools package discovery in `pyproject.toml`, configure `[tool.setuptools.packages.find]` with an explicit `include` allowlist of the intended top-level package(s) rather than relying on defaults (which treat everything as implicit namespaces) or using `exclude`/`namespaces = false`. Omit the packaging configuration entirely when setuptools defaults already produce the correct build/install behavior.
reason: setuptools treats implicit namespaces as package candidates by default under pyproject.toml, causing directories like `docs/` and `tests/` to leak into wheels; disabling namespaces produces warnings for importable non-package directories. An explicit include allowlist fails closed against newly added directories and avoids both problems, while still not over-configuring when defaults are sufficient.
common_pattern: Correct configuration of setuptools package discovery — choosing explicit vs. default packaging entries, using an allowlist, and using the correct directive syntax in docs/examples.

text: Prefer `pyproject.toml` for Python tool configuration when the tool supports it; otherwise use a dedicated tool-specific config file (e.g., `.flake8`). Do not overload `setup.cfg` with non-setuptools configuration—reserve it for setuptools metadata.
reason: `setup.cfg` semantically belongs to setuptools; mixing unrelated tool config there conflates ownership, confuses other tools that read `setup.cfg`, and obscures the preferred modern configuration location (`pyproject.toml`). When a tool like flake8 lacks `pyproject.toml` support, a dedicated file (`.flake8`) or a compatible alternative keeps configuration clean and discoverable.
common_pattern: Proper organization and correctness of Python tool configuration files: keep tool-specific config separate from setuptools metadata, prefer pyproject.toml when supported, and ensure exact section names.

text: Section/header names in build/config files (e.g., `setup.cfg`, `pyproject.toml`, ini files) must exactly match the names expected by the consuming tool; a typo causes the section to be silently ignored.
reason: Tools like setuptools match section headers by exact string; misspelled sections (e.g., `[optoins.extras_require]`) are ignored without warning, silently dropping the intended configuration.
common_pattern: Proper organization and correctness of Python tool configuration files: keep tool-specific config separate from setuptools metadata, prefer pyproject.toml when supported, and ensure exact section names.

text: For release artifact builds, use `python -m build` without `--wheel` or `--sdist` flags so the wheel is built from the sdist, verifying sdist-to-wheel buildability.
reason: The default build flow validates that the sdist can be used to build wheels; passing `--wheel` forces the wheel to be built from the source tree, losing that verification.
common_pattern: Proper handling of wheels in Python packaging: ensuring wheels are built from sdist during release builds and installing the wheel package in CI to avoid legacy setup.py installs.

text: Populate debug-only query metadata (e.g. `executed_query`) only when `settings.DEBUG` is True, rather than unconditionally during query execution.
reason: Avoids unnecessary connection/router access and prevents test failures in environments where debug query capture is disabled or unavailable.
common_pattern: Django `--debug-sql` / `django.db.backends` query logging: how backend SQL formatting hooks, debug-only metadata, docs, and tests interact in the debug SQL pipeline.

text: For Django Meta options that accept lists of objects (e.g., Meta.constraints), add a system check that validates each member against the expected base class (e.g., BaseConstraint), but restrict the check to exact base classes or otherwise preserve custom subclass semantics to avoid rejecting valid subclasses.
reason: Invalid Meta entries can be silently accepted and fail later, so an explicit check provides a clear validation error and enforces the option's type contract; however, broad isinstance checks that include custom subclasses can cause regressions when identical conditions are intentional.
common_pattern: Adding system checks to validate Django Meta options (e.g., Meta.constraints) against expected base classes while preserving custom subclass semantics.

text: In admin list filters, sentinel/default query parameters (e.g. `list_filter_sentinel`) should only be emitted when the corresponding ModelAdmin actually defines defaults; when no defaults exist, omit the sentinel from filter state and query strings.
reason: Filters know about the sentinel but not the ModelAdmin defaults; tying sentinel usage to real defaults prevents meaningless sentinel query parameters, preserves backwards-compatible link behavior, and avoids unnecessary test churn.
scope: admin list filter link / query-string generation
common_pattern: Implementation conventions for Django admin list filters (django/contrib/admin/filters.py and the changelist filter machinery): deriving filter behavior from model field metadata rather than type checks, keeping querystring parameters decoupled from ORM lookups, gating sentinel/active-filter flags on real configuration/state, and avoiding extra DB queries during filter construction.

text: Set `can_group_by_geometry = False` for the Oracle spatial backend because Oracle cannot GROUP BY LOB values.
reason: Prevents generating invalid Oracle SQL with geometry/LOB expressions in GROUP BY (ticket-24096).
common_pattern: Oracle GIS/spatial backend rules: the Oracle spatial backend has behavioral constraints (unsupported SRID, LOB-based geometry, manual `as_oracle()` handling) that must be reflected correctly in its function mappings, backend flags, and documentation.

text: Gate backend-specific optimizations on a `DatabaseFeatures` capability flag (e.g. support for tuple `IN` subqueries) instead of unconditionally pre-selecting idents in the composite-PK path.
reason: Backends differ in expression support; a feature flag lets capable backends avoid the pre-selection work while keeping a safe fallback for others.
common_pattern: Django composite-primary-key handling: treat the composite key as a set of constituent fields, applying per-field checks (defaults, nulls) rather than operating on the aggregate PK or a sliced tuple. Secondary sub-patterns cover backend-capability detection and keeping special-value conditions local to their operation.

text: In system checks for optional settings, accept `None` as a valid value and only flag non-`None` values that fail the expected type check; add test coverage for the `None` case. When iterating a settings mapping, validate keys independently of value-specific `None` handling (a `None` value does not make an invalid key valid).
reason: Optional settings may be intentionally unset or explicitly `None` to disable a feature; treating `None` as an error creates false-positives, while skipping iteration on `None` values can hide invalid keys.
common_pattern: Django system checks as the canonical mechanism for validating configuration/settings: when to add them (documented requirements, nested-dict settings, coordinated security settings), where they belong (checks framework rather than Settings.__init__ or shared docs), and how to write them defensively (accept None for optional settings, validate keys independent of value handling, prefer any() over all()).

text: Pin browser driver versions (e.g. ChromeDriver) in CI workflows so Selenium runs are deterministic. When a helper needs a workaround for a driver-version quirk, prefer pinning a compatible driver in CI over broadly suppressing `WebDriverException`.
reason: Unpinned drivers change exception behavior between versions and cause flaky failures; broad exception suppression hides unrelated Selenium errors, whereas pinning addresses the root cause and preserves meaningful test failures.
common_pattern: Selenium/browser test infrastructure concerns in Django's runner: validating driver availability without side effects, distinguishing failure kinds, keeping drivers deterministic in CI, and correctly skipping unsupported capabilities. The cluster is loosely unified by 'Selenium test setup/validation' but contains distinct sub-patterns, including a genuine instantiate-vs-import contradiction within PR#6272 that is resolved by the import+issubclass approach (2 votes, with the strongest side-effect rationale).

text: When changing the test runner CLI (flags, settings, verbosity, warnings, input handling) or adding a non-default test configuration, update all relevant CI workflows/builders to pass the equivalent explicit arguments, and exercise non-default configurations in scheduled/non-PR CI runs so they do not silently diverge or go untested.
reason: Keeps CI jobs consistent and comparable, prevents silent configuration drift after CLI changes, and ensures added configurations are actually exercised without slowing every PR.
common_pattern: CI test-runner invocations must be kept in sync with test runner CLI semantics and with all supported configurations, including non-default configurations that are exercised outside the default PR matrix.

text: Declare ESLint global variables directly in the ESLint configuration file (e.g., `eslint.config.js`) rather than adding an external package like `globals` as a dev dependency.
reason: Avoids requiring `npm install` for pre-commit hooks to work, keeps configuration self-contained, and reduces dependency management overhead.
common_pattern: Correctly declaring global identifiers for JavaScript linters/ESLint so that the declarations are self-contained and syntactically valid, whether in ESLint configuration or inline `/*global ... */` directive comments.

text: Provide Django system checks for CSP-nonce misconfiguration: when CSP middleware is enabled with `CSP.NONCE` in the policy, warn/error if the nonce is never going to reach a header (e.g. `CSP.NONCE` absent from all configured header directives, or `django.template.context_processors.csp` missing from `TEMPLATES['OPTIONS']['context_processors']`).
reason: These misconfigurations silently break the header/content nonce match and render in templates without ever appearing in a CSP header, making failures hard to diagnose.
common_pattern: This cluster is unified by its domain — Django's CSP nonce middleware and its documentation — but it contains several distinct sub-patterns: (1) caching of nonce-bearing responses (`Cache-Control: private` vs `no_store`), (2) persisting/reading the generated nonce on the request object and respecting lazy-object semantics, (3) documentation of nonce behavior (matching requirement, access-based header emission, placement/structure of `Nonce Usage`), and (4) system checks for common CSP-nonce misconfigurations.

text: Django security-header settings should map directly to the HTTP header they configure: expose semantically distinct policies as separate settings, use flat dictionaries whose keys/values match the header contents rather than wrapper or mode sub-keys, accept either a single value or a sequence for headers that allow multiple policy tokens and serialize sequences as comma-separated header values, and have documentation cross-reference the specific header or policy anchor rather than a generic one.
reason: Comments across PRs converge on treating security-header settings as direct representations of the corresponding HTTP headers, both in configuration shape and documentation references.
common_pattern: Django security-header configuration should mirror the HTTP header it configures: distinct policies become distinct settings, values map directly to header contents, multi-token headers support sequence fallbacks, and documentation references the specific header/policy anchor.

text: When migrating configuration from global settings to per-provider or per-component options, make defaults and fallbacks explicit: provider-sourced instances should use provider options plus class/component defaults without blending in deprecated global settings, while non-provider instances may fall back to legacy settings or historical defaults so existing configurations keep working; pass required values explicitly through the configuration rather than relying on a component's backward-compatibility fallback.
reason: Preserves backward compatibility during configuration refactors while keeping the new provider/option path self-contained and deterministic, avoiding surprising behavior from mixed configuration sources.
scope: Django configuration backends/loaders (mail providers, template engines)
common_pattern: Explicit, backward-compatible default/fallback handling when configuration moves from global settings to per-provider or per-component options. The cluster combines complementary halves: provider-sourced configuration should not blend with deprecated global settings, while non-provider paths may still fall back to legacy settings or historical defaults. The apparent tension between falling back to legacy settings and using class/component defaults is resolved by keeping configuration sources mutually exclusive.

text: For Django settings mappings that map aliases to independent configurations (e.g. EMAIL_PROVIDERS, STORAGES), populate standard defaults in code via setdefault/default dicts, treat optional nested mappings such as OPTIONS as optional when absent, and only raise ImproperlyConfigured for missing required keys, naming the missing alias/key in the error message.
reason: This preserves Django's convention of reporting configuration errors clearly while making configuration ergonomic: users and tests should not need to restate default aliases or empty optional sections just to override one alias.
common_pattern: Django settings mappings that map aliases to independent configurations should supply sensible defaults in code for optional nested mappings, so users/tests can specify minimal configuration; only genuinely required keys should raise ImproperlyConfigured with an actionable message naming the missing key/alias.

text: When translating a settings value between scalar and collection forms (e.g., SECRET_KEY/SECRET_KEYS), explicitly handle empty/falsy source values by assigning the corresponding empty/default derived value; do not wrap a falsy scalar in a list or index an empty collection.
reason: The two PR #13618 generalizations are complementary halves: falsy scalar -> collection must clear the derived setting, and empty collection -> scalar must assign the empty scalar value rather than indexing the first element.
common_pattern: Empty/falsy values in Django settings are special cases: they must be handled or documented according to the specific setting's semantics rather than assumed to behave like ordinary values or copied from another setting.

text: When a management command reads project configuration from pyproject.toml under [tool.django], any runtime paths derived from that configuration (e.g., sys.path entries) should also be configurable in the same [tool.django] section, defaulting to the pyproject.toml parent directory if the key is not set.
reason: Keeps project layout configuration in one place and avoids hardcoding assumptions about the current working directory as the import root.
common_pattern: Configuration for runtime paths derived from Django settings should be exposed in the same [tool.django] section of pyproject.toml, with a sensible default when absent.

text: For password-hashing secrets such as peppers, store secrets as an immutable versioned collection (version-to-value mapping or ordered version/value pairs); persist the secret version alongside each password hash; during verification, resolve the secret by the stored version; and for new credentials, use the highest available version. This enables gradual secret/pepper rotation without invalidating existing hashes.
reason: Allows old hashes to continue verifying with their original secret version while new hashes move to newer secrets during rotation.
scope: Password hashing and versioned secret/pepper rotation design
common_pattern: Versioned secret rotation for password hashing: maintain a version-to-secret mapping, persist the selected version alongside each hash, resolve the matching secret during verification, and use the newest version for new credentials.

text: For MySQL SQL mode handling in Django docs and backend validation, refer to specific SQL modes (e.g., ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, STRICT_ALL_TABLES) rather than describing the contents of the sql_mode option or checking composite modes like TRADITIONAL.
reason: Specific SQL mode names make conditions clearer in docs and avoid redundant checks in validation because MySQL expands composite modes into their constituent strict flags.
scope: MySQL backend validation and MySQL-related documentation
common_pattern: Precise, version-aware handling of MySQL SQL mode in Django docs and backend validation: refer to specific SQL modes rather than sql_mode contents or composite modes, and document version-specific default behavior.

text: When selecting a matching handler from an ordered list of handlers (e.g., Django logging handlers), use the first match in the list rather than the last, and do not add a system check for multiple matches; the defined order provides deterministic selection.
reason: Handlers are provided in an ordered array/list, so the first match reflects the defined order. Choosing the last is arbitrary. Adding a system check for ambiguity is overkill and may rely on assumptions about logging configuration internals.
common_pattern: Selecting a matching handler from an ordered list: prefer the first match and avoid adding a system check for ambiguity.

text: Apply view-type-specific form options correctly: gate add-only options such as `prepopulated_fields` to the add view, and when computing view-level flags like `is_multipart()` check the main admin form and every inline admin formset's form, not just the main form.
reason: Passing add-only options to the change view is unnecessary and misleading, and ignoring inline formsets when computing `is_multipart()` renders the form without multipart encoding, silently breaking inline file uploads.
common_pattern: Django admin form/formset handling must remain consistent across request phases and account for inline formsets: the same permission-aware formset construction used for GET rendering must be used for POST processing (with POST-only filtering appropriately guarded and failed validation rendering the same inlines), and view-level form configuration must be appropriate to the view type and include inline formsets.

text: Coverage exclusions in `tests/.coveragerc` must be narrow: do not exclude ordinary methods (e.g., `def __repr__`) and avoid blanket `exclude_lines` patterns (e.g., `raise AssertionError`) that also match legitimate, coverable code. Scope exclusions to specific defensive/unreachable patterns or specific files.
reason: Excluding methods or blanket lines from coverage hides untested behavior and weakens the coverage signal, reducing confidence in code paths that may contain logic worth validating.
common_pattern: Coverage exclusion configuration should be narrowly scoped to genuinely unreachable/defensive code rather than used to suppress ordinary, coverable code paths.

text: Backend getters/accessors should instantiate the backend only once, cache the instance after first construction, and invalidate/rebuild the cached instance when the relevant backend setting changes.
reason: Instantiating the backend on every call is unnecessary overhead and does not follow the lifecycle/caching pattern used by other backend implementations.
common_pattern: Design principles for Django cache backend implementations: placing behavior at the correct level of the cache backend class hierarchy, keeping backend-specific helpers encapsulated, preserving concurrency/atomicity guarantees, and managing backend instance lifecycle consistently across backends.

text: In backend-specific database code, when branching on a field type or column type, cover every type that maps to the same underlying backend storage type rather than matching a single type. For Oracle, NCLOB/CLOB handling must include both `TextField` and `JSONField`, JSONField should be converted via the TextField path, and large text/JSON fields should map to `NCLOB` (national character set), not `CLOB`. Prefer a shared module-level constant or suffix/`endswith` matching (e.g. MySQL `('blob', 'text')`) over narrow, per-type enumeration so new variants are not missed.
reason: A field type silently excluded from backend-specific handling causes incorrect SQL (e.g. JSON null scalar extraction in `IN` queries) or missing Unicode support on the affected backend.
scope: Django database backends: Oracle (`oracle/base.py`, `oracle/operations.py`, `functions/comparison.py`) and MySQL (`mysql/schema.py`, `validation.py`).
common_pattern: When writing backend-specific database code, branches on column/field types must account for every field type that maps to the same underlying backend storage type (and, conversely, tests/queries must avoid field types the backend disallows in certain constructs like IN()). Groups 1/3/4/2 cover the 'cover all equivalent field types' half; 6/7/8 cover 'enumerate exhaustively / reuse a shared constant'; 5 is the anti-pattern consequence.

text: Every job in GitHub Actions workflow files (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) should include `timeout-minutes: 60`.
reason: Prevents CI jobs from running indefinitely, bounds resource usage, and maintains consistency across workflow files.
common_pattern: GitHub Actions workflow configuration hygiene in `.github/workflows/*.yml` — both generalizations prescribe specific settings for workflow files to improve reliability and shared-infrastructure courtesy, though they address distinct aspects (job timeouts vs. scheduled cron timing).

text: In packaging metadata (`pyproject.toml`/`setup.cfg`), declare licenses explicitly and completely: list actual license files individually in `license-files` (avoid `LICENSE*` globs and non-license files such as `AUTHORS`), use exact SPDX identifiers (e.g., `BSD-3-Clause`) in `license` instead of ambiguous labels like `BSD`, express multiple bundled licenses with SPDX expressions (e.g., `BSD-3-Clause AND Python-2.0`), and add matching Trove `License :: ...` classifiers when additional licensing applies.
reason: These practices keep package license metadata unambiguous, machine-readable, and accurate for built distributions and package indexes.
common_pattern: Packaging license metadata should be explicit, standardized, and complete: use exact SPDX identifiers or expressions, list actual license files explicitly, and add matching license classifiers when additional licensing applies.

text: In automation/CI shell scripts (e.g., `scripts/*.sh`), invoke every git command that can trigger repository hooks (e.g., `commit`, `commit --amend`, `cherry-pick`, `merge`, `rebase`) as `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null <command>`, applying the suppression consistently to all such commands in the script so hooks cannot block or mutate the automated flow.
reason: Hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, post-commit, etc.) can fail or rewrite history in contexts where they are unwanted, making automation non-deterministic; but disabling them for only some git invocations leaves the remaining commands still hook-driven and reintroduces the original failure mode.
common_pattern: Both generalizations address the same concern: when git commands are run non-interactively from automation/CI shell scripts, repository hooks must be suppressed via `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null` (or an equivalent flag), and this suppression must be applied consistently to *every* hook-triggering git command in the script, not just the one that originally surfaced the problem.

text: In `.github/workflows/tests.yml`, keep at least one job that runs with latest/unpinned dependencies on pushes to `main`, not on PRs, so upstream breakage is caught without adding unrelated noise to PR checks.
reason: Latest-dependency jobs surface upstream breakage; running them only on main avoids PR noise from failures unrelated to the change.
common_pattern: Strategies for managing CI dependencies to balance catching upstream breakage with keeping PR checks stable.

text: CI workflow steps and scripts under `scripts/` should not depend on a non-root `working-directory`; make scripts resolve paths relative to their own location, accept explicit path arguments, or otherwise run correctly from the repository root.
reason: Avoids hidden current-working-directory assumptions, makes CI and local invocation consistent, and simplifies workflow configuration.
common_pattern: Keeping CI/automation logic robust and testable: derivations of 'don't embed fragile logic in workflow YAML or rely on implicit execution context — put it in standalone, testable, lintable files with explicit path handling.' Two distinct sub-patterns: (a) extracting inline workflow scripts (2 converging generalizations), (b) not depending on a non-root working directory (1 generalization).

text: Gate functional/expression index SQL on explicit backend feature flags (e.g. `supports_expression_indexes`, with a narrower `supports_expression_indexes_on_columns` for expression indexes over plain columns) and represent the index type with an explicit marker (e.g. `Index.is_functional`) rather than inspecting expressions; emit such indexes only when the active connection supports them.
reason: Backend capabilities vary (e.g. MySQL rejects functional indexes on a column with error 3762), so SQL generation must branch on feature support, and an explicit marker avoids fragile expression parsing.
common_pattern: Handling of expression/functional indexes: never clobber caller-supplied index expressions, and gate backend-specific expression-index behavior on explicit, capability-based feature flags (with an explicit index-type marker rather than fragile expression inspection).

text: For periodic maintenance tasks in shared cache/database backends (e.g. cache culling), do not rely on per-instance counters, because independent instances can synchronize counters and trigger bursts of maintenance ops. Instead de-synchronize instances: either stagger the timing deterministically per instance so the expected number of executions over the population is guaranteed (independent random sampling with replacement does not guarantee proportional coverage), or if using a probabilistic trigger, check `random.random()` against a configurable frequency ratio and default that ratio to `1` so maintenance still runs on every call.
reason: Per-instance counters advance independently and can align, producing clustered culls; independent random draws give variable/proportional-underguaranteed outcomes, so either deterministic staggering or a tunable probabilistic check (with a default-preserving ratio) is needed to control cadence without synchronization.
common_pattern: How to trigger periodic maintenance tasks (e.g. cache culling) in a shared backend across multiple independent instances without synchronization side-effects — avoiding per-instance counters (which can align and cause bursts) and controlling how often/when the maintenance runs.

text: Validate or apply normalization for invariant cache backend configuration such as key_prefix once in __init__ rather than repeating it on every call in the hot path (e.g. make_key()).
reason: key_prefix does not change per call, so validating it per-operation wastes work on a hot path and duplicates warnings; initialization is the correct place for invariant configuration checks.
common_pattern: Django cache backend key handling: how make_key/validate_key/key_prefix are implemented, tested, and kept backwards-compatible (including during deprecation of non-string keys). The cluster splits into three distinct sub-patterns: (a) testing key validation through public behavior rather than mocks, (b) deprecation-safe non-string key handling, and (c) where invariant key configuration is validated.

text: Expose hard-coded database-backend test-database creation parameters (e.g., Oracle tablespace/datafile sizing) as tunable TEST.* settings, and name new settings consistently with existing related options including their temporary-resource variants (e.g., if DATAFILE_MAXSIZE / DATAFILE_TMP_MAXSIZE exist, name new ones DATAFILE_SIZE / DATAFILE_EXTSIZE / DATAFILE_TMP_SIZE / DATAFILE_TMP_EXTSIZE).
reason: Allows users to tune backend test-database resource sizing without code changes and keeps the settings API consistent and discoverable.
scope: Django database backend test database creation settings
common_pattern: Django database-backend test-database creation: configuring it via discoverable settings, centralizing parameter construction in shared helpers, and defensively computing derived values — all to avoid hardcoding, duplication, and invalid test-DB config.

text: Avoid wildcard `ALLOWED_HOSTS` entries (`ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']`) in tests and testing documentation: in tests, override `ALLOWED_HOSTS` with the explicit hostnames required by the test rather than a wildcard; in documentation, explain why permissive wildcard settings are discouraged instead of only showing the recommended alternative.
reason: Explicit hostnames document test dependencies and keep tests consistent with host-redirect behavior tests; documenting the wildcard rationale helps readers understand the recommendation and avoid unsafe shortcuts.
common_pattern: Both generalizations govern the use and explanation of wildcard `ALLOWED_HOSTS` settings: tests should use explicit hostnames instead of `['*']`, and documentation should explain why the permissive wildcard is discouraged rather than only presenting the recommended alternative.

text: Reuse existing ModelAdmin display-limit options (such as `delete_confirmation_max_display`) for inline/protected-error rendering instead of adding separate inline-specific constants, and ensure the shared option applies to inline paths as well as `ModelAdmin` paths.
reason: Avoids duplicate configuration, keeps related admin interfaces behaviorally consistent, and honors documented/configurable limits across both model admin and inline rendering.
common_pattern: Reuse existing configurable Django admin display-limit options across related admin rendering paths, including inlines, instead of introducing parallel constants or leaving some paths unlimited.

text: On settings wrappers such as Django's LazySettings, keep the exposed public API limited to documented/replacement settings: filter deprecated setting names from __dir__/introspection when their replacement setting is defined, and remove undocumented duplicate accessors/aliases in favor of the existing documented attribute.
reason: Both generalizations concern settings-wrapper API hygiene: hiding deprecated settings from introspection and eliminating undocumented duplicate accessors so consumers only see supported settings.
common_pattern: Settings wrapper/API hygiene: avoid exposing deprecated, duplicate, or otherwise unavailable settings/accessors through the settings object.

text: When a PR-quality script uses a size threshold to exempt small PRs from checks (e.g., `LARGE_PR_THRESHOLD` in `scripts/pr_quality/check_pr.py`), set the threshold conservatively low — single digits such as `9`, not `80`. Do not add typo-fix carve-outs for drive-by contributors; small PRs should still go through the standard review requirements until the contribution process stabilizes.
reason: A high threshold creates a broad exception that lets typo-fix PRs bypass quality checks; the project prefers strict enforcement over carve-outs for drive-by contributors.
common_pattern: All three generalizations derive from a single reviewer comment about the PR-quality size-exemption threshold: they agree that the threshold must be kept conservatively low (single digits) so small/typo-fix PRs are not carved out from normal quality requirements.

text: For external HTTP requests (e.g., GitHub API, Trac API), always specify an explicit timeout with a sensible default to prevent indefinite hangs. Use a module-level constant (e.g., `TRAC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`) for simple cases. When you are already changing a timeout or anticipate tuning needs, expose it as a configurable environment variable (e.g., `DJANGO_<COMPONENT>_TIMEOUT`) with a sensible default rather than hardcoding a numeric literal, to future-proof without ongoing churn.
reason: Merges the complementary guidance from all three generalizations: explicit timeouts prevent hangs, fixed constants avoid premature configuration surface, and env vars are warranted when a timeout is already being modified.
common_pattern: Explicit timeout configuration for external HTTP requests: always set a sensible default to avoid indefinite hangs, and conditionally expose it as a configurable environment variable when the timeout is already being modified or tuning is expected.

text: Choose `chunk_size` based on the specific operation's expected cardinality and performance profile rather than reusing a large bulk-serialization batch size (e.g. 2000) for unrelated work such as form choice iteration; prefer reusing established chunk-size constants like `GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE`, or expose `chunk_size` so callers can tune batching themselves.
reason: Different operations have different row counts and memory/latency tradeoffs; a large serialization chunk size can over-fetch for interactive form rendering, while hard-coding sizes diverges from established query-fetching behavior and removes caller control.
common_pattern: Both generalizations address the appropriate selection of `chunk_size` when batching work: choose the chunk size for the specific operation's cardinality/performance profile, and prefer reusing established constants (e.g., `GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE`) or exposing `chunk_size` to callers rather than blindly copying a large batch size from an unrelated use case.

text: When resolving translated URLs or comparing the active language to the configured default language, first apply the supported-language fallback logic to the language code (whether it comes from the URL path or settings.LANGUAGE_CODE) before deciding whether a localized route applies or falling back to the original URL.
reason: Prevents incorrect URL fallback or language-prefix/default-language decisions when a language code is ambiguous in the path or when the configured default is not itself present in the supported languages.
scope: Django language and URL resolution code
common_pattern: Before making language-based URL or default-language decisions, resolve the relevant language code through the supported-language fallback logic rather than assuming the code is directly supported or unambiguous.

text: In tox.ini (and similar ini/config files), format long comma-separated list values such as `passenv` across multiple lines when they exceed a reasonable line length, and match the existing separator style used elsewhere in the file while keeping the syntax valid for tox.
reason: Keeping long list values on one line hurts readability and reviewability; consistent formatting avoids parser ambiguity and accidental inclusion of separators in the parsed list.
scope: file-specific: tox.ini / ini config list values
common_pattern: Formatting conventions for tox.ini configuration entries: readability and consistency for multi-line list values, and conventional spacing for setenv assignments.

text: In tox.ini `setenv` entries, write environment variable assignments without spaces around `=` (`VAR=value`) when the tox version supports it; otherwise follow the spacing shown in official tox docs/examples (`VAR = value`).
reason: Conventional environment-variable syntax omits spaces, but tox docs/examples often show spaces, so compatibility and documented style should be verified before changing.
common_pattern: Formatting conventions for tox.ini configuration entries: readability and consistency for multi-line list values, and conventional spacing for setenv assignments.

text: In docs/conf.py, keep the Sphinx mock-module and Django-app lists minimal — include only entries that resolve an actual import/viewcode warning (verify by removing each entry and confirming the warning returns) — and add a comment stating the selection criterion so maintainers know why some modules/apps are listed and others are omitted.
reason: Undocumented, blanket mock/app lists are opaque and hard to maintain; tying each entry to a concrete build warning and recording the selection rule makes the configuration auditable and lets future maintainers know when entries can be added or removed.
common_pattern: Configuring Sphinx documentation builds (docs/conf.py): the mocks/apps lists should be minimal (only entries justified by a real build/import warning) and each list must carry a comment stating the selection criterion — merging the 'keep it minimal' and 'document why these entries' halves into one maintenance discipline.

text: Expose test configuration (such as browser specs) as class attributes on the test class/metaclass, populated from environment variables in the test runner so users can override values per test class or subclass. Define attribute semantics explicitly (e.g. singular `browser` = the primary/first browser; plural `browsers` = the remaining requested browsers, documented as excluding the primary). Do not carry over configuration attributes from unrelated integrations that the backend does not use.
reason: Supports per-class customization and project-wide reuse while keeping environment parsing out of metaclass construction; clear singular/plural semantics and removal of unused attributes avoid ambiguity and misleading readers about unsupported functionality.
scope: Django test infrastructure / Selenium test base classes
common_pattern: Conventions for constructing Django Selenium/browser-based test classes: how to expose test configuration (browser specs) as class attributes and how to manage the lifecycle of expensive shared resources (WebDriver instances) at class/configuration scope rather than per test.

text: In CI scripts that launch containers, use Docker user-defined networks and container/service DNS names for inter-container communication; use `docker port <container>` for host-accessible endpoints; and use `docker-compose` for multi-service setups — instead of extracting and injecting container IPs with `docker inspect`.
reason: User-defined Docker networks and docker-compose provide built-in DNS resolution and declarative port mapping; container IPs are network-scoped, ephemeral, and require brittle parsing, making service wiring more robust when Docker abstractions are used instead.
common_pattern: CI workflows that wire up external service containers should rely on Docker's own abstractions (user-defined networks/DNS, port mapping, compose) and pinned image versions rather than brittle manual IP extraction or floating tags.

text: When registering psycopg2 range adapters and migration serializers in django.contrib.postgres, cover all concrete psycopg2 range subclasses (DateRange, DateTimeRange, DateTimeTZRange, NumericRange) but exclude the base Range type, and remap the private module psycopg2._range to the public psycopg2.extras so generated migrations import the publicly documented API.
reason: psycopg2 registers adapters for the four concrete subclasses (the base Range has none), and generated migrations should never contain `import psycopg2._range` — the public range API is exposed through psycopg2.extras. Auditing all analogous range fields prevents partial serialization support.
